characters: the two blue pigs (sow and shoat)
events: At the end of a hot spring day Gus shoos the blue pigs (who are eating a rattlesnake) off the porch, fetches his whiskey jug from the springhouse and settles in to drink toward sundown.
Call and Pea Eye come up from the lots, then an exhausted Newt; they have hit rock digging the new well, and Call's temper is bad because his mare bit a chunk out of his side.

Bolivar pounds the clapperless dinner bell with a broken crowbar; over sowbelly and beans Gus needles Call with riverboat and whore stories while Call privately judges that the quarter 'rustler's moon' makes it time to raid Mexico for stock.
A squabble over who freed the slaves ends with Gus teasing that Scottish-born Call is no American; Call takes his hat and Henry rifle and walks out into the night.
season: Spring (text calls it a quiet spring evening; cattlemen are making up their spring herds). A very dry year. Moon is in the quarter. Era: roughly a decade after the Civil War (late 1870s per most readings; the novel does not give a year here).

notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: the blue pigs; Gus's jug in the springhouse; the Hell Bitch (named, described); the clapperless dinner bell and broken crowbar; Call's Henry rifle. Backstory mentions: Stone House fight with the Keechis (Pea Eye's deaf ear) and walking down the Brazos; Prairie Dog Fork of the Red. Pickles Gap is a (fictional) settlement twelve miles off. GradeSaver misspells the barber 'Dillan'; the text has Dillard Brawley.

scenes.action: The blue sow and shoat play tug-of-war with a small rattlesnake on the porch until Gus kicks them off.
Gus waits in the sun for a coiled rattler to leave, then lifts his burlap-wrapped jug out of the mud and checks it for centipedes before a swig.

scenes.action: Sweat-blackened Call and Pea Eye, then a mud-caked Newt, trudge up from the lots past the wagons as Gus offers the jug.

scenes.action: Bolivar treats the bite above Call's belt; Gus grabs seconds of beans; the talk sours and Call stands in the doorway with his Henry and leaves.

visualDetails: Hat Creek 'offices' = a roofless barn (roof blown off three years earlier) and a couple of patched corrals; wagons in the yard; a little lumpy adobe springhouse; a blacksmith's shop with a forge; a dinner bell with no clapper.
No shade tree within twenty or thirty miles; chaparral flats, dust, horned toads, roadrunners.
The pigs are blue: an old sow and a young shoat; the shoat trails Gus 'quiet as a cat' and eats a lizard.

The Hell Bitch: Call's mare, bought in Mexico; dapple gray; white muzzle; white blaze/streak on the forehead; taller than an Indian pony, shorter-barreled than a thoroughbred; vicious — once kicked Newt into the blacksmith shop.
Call: barely middle-sized but seems big; Gus four inches taller; Pea Eye three inches taller than Gus — tall, lank, awkward-looking, deaf in the left ear, prominent Adam's apple.
Bolivar: old ex-bandit, dirty serape, lard-greasy hair, waxed mustache; drinks brown sugar with a little coffee.
Call's rifle is a Henry; Gus also owns a Henry. Supper: sowbelly and chili beans; goat Gus says tastes fried in tar.

events: Call walks the river alone for an hour, as he does every night, sitting at the old Comanche crossing; he admits to himself there is no real threat and that he is weary of being 'the Captain' of a small livery business with no troop and no war.

On the porch Bolivar whets his bone-handled knife, trades insults with Gus about wives and daughters, and throws the knife into a wagon side; Newt frets that the two old fighters might someday have a real fight.
Newt privately dwells on his silent love for Lorena Wood, the Dry Bean's whore, whom he has never dared speak to.

Call returns, says it would have been a good night to cross stock; he again puts off Newt's request to ride on a raid, and Gus heads to town to gamble while Call warns him not to let 'that girl' talk him into marriage.

scenes.weather: peaceful and still; Dry Bean piano faintly audible
scenes.action: Bolivar's thin blade flashes in the moonlight on the whetstone; he flings the knife and it quivers in a wagon twenty feet away while Gus twirls his Colt's cylinder.
Newt, hunched on the bottom step, scratches the friendly shoat's ears and daydreams about what he will say to Lorena; Pea Eye snores against the railing.
Call returns with his rifle in the crook of his arm and lights a smoke; Newt is sent to bed; Gus steps over the sleeping shoat and walks off toward the saloon.

visualDetails: Bolivar's knife: fine bone-handled knife, handle of mule-deer horn, thin blade; he spits on the whetstone.
Pea Eye's 'Sunday knife': a Bowie with a fourteen-inch blade in a big sheath.
Gus: Colt revolver in a holster hung on the chair back; an old silver pocket watch, pencil stub and notebook kept in the old black vest he always wears (he times Bolivar urinating).
The Dry Bean's piano has wheels; deacons built a ramp and a board track so it can be pushed next door to the church on Sundays; once it derailed and lost two legs and was played in the street.
Lorena lives upstairs over the Dry Bean and uses its back stairs.
Bolivar once gave Newt a serape to use as a blanket; Newt sleeps in a bunk above Bolivar's.
Lippy Jones plays the piano and has an unhealed bullet hole in his belly.

characters: Augustus McCrae (in her recollection of a July visit)
events: Lorena, nearly twenty-four and stuck in hot Lonesome Dove, fixes on San Francisco as the cool place she means to reach; Gus's long talk about the city is part of why.

Her history: orphaned at seventeen in Baton Rouge, taken by Mosby Marlin to a windowless, mosquito-plagued house near Gladewater and prostituted to pay his debts; rescued/bought by the handsome gambler John Tinkersley, who took her to a San Antonio hotel, beat her and pimped her.

On the way to the border she tried to shoot Tinkersley with an uncocked gun, clubbed his jaw instead, and he bit her upper lip (her small scar); he abandoned her penniless in Lonesome Dove, calling her murderous, and she cooked for Xavier at the Dry Bean until Gus became her first customer.
(Memory) One blistering July day Gus paid her ten dollars in gold simply to hear her life story; she declined, returned the coin, and they went down to play cards.
season: Present frame not dated (implicitly the same spring); the $10 conversation is a memory from a previous July.

visualDetails: Lorena: nearly 24, blonde (hair colour is established elsewhere; here: 'developed well', very pretty), faint small scar just above her upper lip from Tinkersley's bite; habitually silent.
Gus: a mass of white hair (turned white at thirty); always wears spurs, even off horseback; rides a big black horse 'that could pull three stagecoaches'; paid her five dollars in gold per visit.
Tinkersley: tallest, prettiest, cleanest man she'd seen; had his fingernails trimmed; middling gambler.
Lorena liked riding a horse with a sidesaddle (Tinkersley sold it).

events: Gus strolls into town under a clear starry sky, straps on his heavy Colt dragoon on the dry creek bed, and is startled by an armadillo.

At the Dry Bean, Xavier (fussy, melancholy Frenchman) snatches Lippy's filthy bowler hat and flings it out the back door; Dish Boggett, broke after losing his wages in Matamoros, has ridden up the river hoping Lorena will give him credit.
Gus reflects that Lorena reminds him of Clara Allen, the woman he loved most; he gets up a card game with Dish, Lippy, Xavier and Lorena, and helps Lorena win so she brightens up.

Outside, Dish says he's signed with Shanghai Pierce's UU outfit; Gus gives him the two dollars he'd asked for and invites him to sleep on the Hat Creek porch; Dish slips up Lorena's back stairs and Gus walks home to find the pigs asleep on the porch.

Dish Boggett: barely 22, walrus mustache the colour of a prairie dog (between yellow and brown); rides a rangy sorrel.
Lorena: fine head of soft blond hair, slightly hollow cheeks, side-looking cloudy eyes, very pale skin; wears cheap powder.

events: Gus rises about 4 a.m., bakes sourdough biscuits in a Dutch oven outside, and reads the Prophets (Amos) on an upturned lard kettle as the sun rises over dewy chaparral; the pigs and a stiff, half-awake Call join him.

Breakfast is chaos: Newt asleep upright with knife and fork, Bolivar sick and spilling coffee grounds into the eggs, Pea Eye and Dish relieving themselves off the back steps; Dish is dazed with love after his night with Lorena.
Call, who has been mulling a trail drive for a year, offers Dish work and announces they are raiding into Mexico that night and may make up a herd; Gus scoffs, Dish agrees to wait a day or two.
From the back porch Call spots two riders far up the San Antonio stage road; Gus recognises Deets on his white gelding and, by his peculiar slump in the saddle, Jake Spoon.
season: Spring; the morning after chapters 1–4. The new well has been six weeks in the digging.

Dish's alternative was a sure job back on the Matagorda (Texas coast). The Hat Creek operation leases just enough land to hold small lots of stock. scenes.action: Gus sits on the big black upturned kettle with his Bible while biscuits brown in the Dutch oven; the rising sun turns dew-wet chaparral into glittering diamonds and rainbows.
Call steps out pulling on his shirt; the dew-damp blue pigs stand in front of Gus as if hoping to eat the Bible; Dish sleeps on the porch with his hat over his eyes and his head on his saddle.
Newt dozes sitting bolt upright with knife and fork; Bolivar spills coffee grounds into the frying eggs; the shoat peers in the doorway.

scenes.action: Two distant riders waver in the heat haze on the straight road; Gus, licking honey off his finger, names them: Deets and Jake Spoon.

A huge black lard kettle, upturned, serves as Gus's morning seat.
Newt has a cowlick; Pea Eye's pants have about fifteen small buttons.

characters: a pig on the back porch
events: Newt is overwhelmed: Jake Spoon was his mother Maggie's kindest visitor, gave him his first ride and first boots, and Newt privately suspects Jake is his father; Jake left ten years ago and Maggie died about a year later.

Jake and a beaming Deets ride into the yard; Jake's pacing bay is ridden down to the bone, which tells Call and Gus he is running from trouble; Call pointedly sets Dish to well-digging to test whether he'll keep his word.
Over fried meat Jake praises Montana — grass, water, buffalo above the Yellowstone — and urges them to beat everyone there with free Texas cattle.

Jake admits he accidentally killed a dentist in Fort Smith, Arkansas, less than three weeks earlier: firing a borrowed buffalo gun at a drunk mule skinner, the bullet went through a plank wall and killed the dentist across the street — who was the mayor and brother of sheriff July Johnson.
Gus drops the remark that one of them (Jake or Call) is probably Newt's father; Call takes his rifle and leaves.
season: Spring, same morning as chapter 5. Jake's killing was 'not three weeks' earlier. Maggie has been dead nine years; Jake left ten years ago.

Deets, in patched quilt pants with cotton ticking poking out and a battered cavalry cap, leads the gaunt horses to the roofless barn.
Jake, face red from scrubbing with a filthy sacking towel, complains about the dirt and the pig on the porch.
Jake daintily picks at his food and a whittled match while telling of Montana and the dead dentist; Call stands in the doorway fidgeting.

Newt keeps a small bundle of his mother's things: beads, combs, a scrapbook, magazine cut-outs, a scratchy picture of his Alabama grandfather.
Fort Smith (per Jake): a pretty river town with wide streets; catfish.

events: Jake and Gus reminisce; Jake reports he glimpsed Clara outside a store in Ogallala — she and horse-trader Bob Allen live on the North Platte in Nebraska, have two girls, and lost their boys.
(Memory) Gus recalls Clara at sixteen: her parents were killed in the great Indian raid of 1856 and she ran their Austin store; she refused both him and Jake and married dull Bob Allen from Kentucky.
Gus and Jake drink from the jug in the springhouse shade until Jake falls asleep with his hat over his face; Gus decides not to tell Jake about Lorena, sure he'll find her.
Gus teases a sweat-soaked Dish at the well windlass, then watches Call snub, blanket and saddle the Hell Bitch, tying up a hind foot so she stands on three legs.
Call abruptly proposes they go north to Montana; Gus mocks it as a wilderness, but warms to it on realising the route crosses the Platte where Clara lives; Call says Newt could run the ranch.

events: In blistering afternoon heat Call rides the lathered mare back from a twenty-mile lope and tells the well-diggers to rest: they are going to Mexico tonight. Newt hopes he's included.
Two riders stop to read Gus's elaborate sign (history told: names added for Pea Eye and for Deets as 'Deets, Joshua', rent/sale lines, 'We Don't Rent Pigs', and a Latin motto Gus can't translate).

The riders are Wilbarger, a trail boss whose remuda was stolen by Mexicans and who needs forty horses for a herd waiting beyond the Nueces bound for Kansas, and his pockmarked hand Chick, who asks for the yellow-haired whore; Dish claims she's his sister.

Dish walks to the Dry Bean and hears Lorena's cornshuck bed creaking with another man; he stalks the town ready to kill, sits by the river an hour, then returns to find her flushed and sharing a glass with Jake Spoon — Jake cheerfully buys him drinks and Dish gets drunk singing at Lippy's piano.

notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: the Hat Creek sign and its Latin motto (full contents given in this chapter); Wilbarger and Chick. Gus is two years older than Call. The motto is Gus's misremembered version of a Latin proverb (usually 'uva uvam videndo varia fit', 'a grape changes colour by seeing another grape'); Gus doesn't know its meaning. Sabinas (Mexico) is mentioned as Dish's joke destination. Juan Cortinas is a real historical figure (Juan Cortina). Study guides agree.

Parker (Wrangler)'; 'Deets, Joshua'; rent line (horses and rigs); sale line (cattle and horses); no goats or donkeys; 'We Don't Rent Pigs'; and the Latin motto 'Uva uvam vivendo varia fit'. The one rentable rig is a spring buggy with no springs, bought from Xavier after it crushed his wife.
Deets: woolly hair just turning gray; big black hands.
Pea Eye's foot is the size and shape of a scoop shovel.
Wilbarger: stocky, red-faced, about Call's age; rides a black horse. Chick: tiny, feisty, deeply pockmarked, big pistol on his leg, rides a nearly swaybacked grulla (mouse-gray); cackling laugh.
Dry Bean: two storeys of frame lumber, swinging doors, hitch rail; Lorena's corner room has a bad bed with a cornshuck mattress.
Jake with hat pushed back shows a strip of sun-untouched white forehead.
Big boys load rolls of barbed wire into a wagon at the Pumphreys' store.

events: Wilbarger rides his black horse right up to the porch (the shoat walks under it); he needs forty broke horses for 3,000 cattle and eleven men; Call promises a hundred horses by sunup at $35 each, only three available today; Wilbarger's brand is HIC on the left hip and he says he studied Latin at Yale.
Call reveals the plan to Gus: raid the Hacienda Flores, largest ranch in Coahuila, sell Wilbarger forty horses and keep the rest as a remuda for a drive north with hired cowboys.

Dish, blind drunk after two bottles with Jake, vomits on hands and knees in Hat Creek; Jake fires three shots over the house to stop Bolivar's bell; Call suspects Gus and Jake set Dish up and lets him ride.
At the lots Call hands Newt his own oiled pistol and gun belt — Newt feels grown for the first time; at sundown the seven-man outfit crosses the river and rides southeast for the Hacienda Flores.
season: Spring, same day as chapters 5–8 (late afternoon to dusk).
herdPosition: n/a - herd not yet assembled
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: Mouse (Newt's dun gelding); Mud Pie (Gus's sorrel); Deets's Walker Colt; Newt's first gun. Note Gus's horse: ch. 3 (Lorena's memory) mentions Gus on a big black horse; here Deets saddles Mud Pie, a sorrel — Gus evidently rides more than one horse. Gus's watch described as silver in ch. 2 and brass here. Dish retches on hands and knees in the dry creek while Gus and Jake chat on the bank; he crawls up the low bank, stands, trips on a mesquite root and falls flat.
As Bolivar clangs the bell early, Jake draws his pearl-handled pistol and fires three shots high over the house; the clanging never stops.

Call steps into the firelight; Sean yells 'murderers', leaps on the hobbled mule and is pitched off, to Deets's delight. The brothers were aiming for Galveston; Call warns that Pedro Flores will hang them and promises to send two horses back for them.

events: Gus's party finds only about forty horses, and they turn out to carry Wilbarger's HIC brand — his stolen remuda; Newt ropes two for the Irishmen and Gus rides off leading them.

They find over a hundred horses in a narrow valley a mile from the hacienda and push them northwest past it; Newt, riding left point alone, broods on hanging and on how crossing the river turns crime into a game.

Near the river the herd collides in the dark with a second herd being run south out of Texas by four Mexican horse thieves; Newt is swept along in the dust-choked stampede, hears Call's Henry fire, and at sunrise finds Call waiting at the Comanche crossing with well over a hundred horses — Newt weeps secretly with relief and only says good morning.

storyline: Hat Creek outfit (with Lorena & Jake subplot)
events: With the prime horses penned, restless Dish convinces himself the bandit threat is imaginary and leaves Deets to guard the corral alone while he goes to the Dry Bean.

Deets, sitting in the shadows against the water trough with his rifle, contentedly watches the thin hook of the moon and muses on his private fears — that Indians understand the moon and might one day ride it or use it to turn the water to salt — and on the sign that made him part of the outfit.

At the Dry Bean Lorena, now retired from whoring and waiting for Jake, beats Dish, Jasper Fant and Xavier at cards; Dish, mesmerised by her white arms, loses three months' wages; Xavier sulks that Jake has robbed his saloon of its draw and him of the woman he loves.
Outside, Jasper — thin, with a shoestring mustache and a scrawny horse — says he'll hire on with the Captain's drive; he and Dish ride back to the pens, both mooning over Lorena.

Lorena insists she will leave when Jake leaves; he proposes San Antonio, Austin or Fort Worth, but she holds to San Francisco and he agrees they will travel alongside the herd, camping separately, toward Denver.
Lorena refuses him further that night and lies awake in the moonlight, already mentally gone from Lonesome Dove.

events: Sheriff July Johnson, 24 and still yellow from jaundice caught at a trial in Missouri, sits outside the Fort Smith jail with his 48-year-old deputy Roscoe Brown, reflecting on his hard year and new marriage.
Peach Johnson, his huge widowed sister-in-law, crosses the street carrying a red rooster and demands to know when he will go after Jake Spoon for killing her husband Benny, the mayor and dentist.
When the rooster pecks her, Peach wrings its neck on the spot and tosses the head into the weeds.
Roscoe recalls the muddled aftermath of the accidental shooting; July, feeling responsible for the town rather than for his unkind brother, resolves he must pursue Jake, likely toward San Antonio.
July walks home at milking time, rejecting Roscoe's request for Joe to come play dominoes.

Lorena bathes chest-deep in the cold green river; a tub-sized snapping turtle on the bank startles her and Jake misses it four times shooting left-handed.
Jake, too sick to manage, collapses on her on the grass; Lorena props him against a tree and starts coffee.
Deets swims his horse across, digs the thorn tip out of Jake's thumb with a heated sewing needle, and warns of a storm and rising river, urging them to cross now.
Deets leads Lorena's balking mare across as it swims; on the far bank he tells her to cook early, douse the fire, and not tie horses to big trees, then rides back to guide Call to the crossing.

scenes.action: Deets glances at the southern sky, gives his storm warnings, and rides into the Nueces for the third time.

visualDetails: The Nueces: green water, cold beneath the surface; shady bank with grass and no mesquite
Snapping turtle as big as a tub
Jake's thumb turned from white to purple; he shoots left-handed and misses four times
White sky overhead; the herd's dust visible far behind to the south from clearings
Deets keeps a large needle in a little packet in his saddlebag for sewing his pants
Lorena's brown mare balks, whirls, shows the whites of her eyes, then swims well
Bedrolls tied high on the horses for the crossing
Jake throws his bedroll under a big mesquite on the far bank

locations: Brush country several miles south of the Nueces River, south Texas: chaparral, mesquite thickets and gullies
Point of the Hat Creek herd on the trail toward the Nueces crossing
events: Deets returns saying a storm is coming and the steep Nueces crossing is too risky in the dark; Call feels a moment of passive uncertainty as a hot south wind rises.
Call sends Newt to tell point riders Dish and Soupy to hold the cattle, but a river of sand sweeps in from the south and the blinded herd stampedes with Newt caught among it.
Mouse carries Newt through tearing mesquite thickets until the brush slows the cattle; in lightning flashes Newt meets Dish, who has lost Soupy.
Blue balls of lightning roll along the cattle's horns and Deets appears to warn Newt to ride away from them.
Torrential rain follows; lost, soaked and cold, Newt lets Mouse plod through floodwater and a gully, hoping for dawn.
season: not stated as a date; Call calls it the stormy time of year. Early in the drive (spring). Same evening as chapter 30.
herdPosition: A few miles south of the Nueces River in the brush country; herd stampeded and scattered in the storm, crossing not yet made
notes: Continuous with ch 30 (same storm Deets predicted). Soupy Jones is separated from the others at chapter's end. GradeSaver says Dish warns Newt away from the lightning-charged cattle; the text has Deets give that warning (Dish only tells him he should have brought a slicker). Newt recalls the dawn after the Mexico horse raid. The Hell Bitch is Call's mount.

scenes.where: Beside the chuck wagon on the trail
scenes.weather: hot south wind rising; sun dark like an eclipse with yellow edges; brown curtain of sand rising west and south; evening star bright above
scenes.action: Gus jokes about a muddy sundown as the Hell Bitch looks round restlessly and Bol digs in the bedrolls for his serape.

scenes.weather: sand beginning to blow; heavy half-light
scenes.action: Slouching Dish grins at the news; Soupy ties his bandana over his nose as snaking streams of sand slide under the cattle's bellies like running wolves.

scenes.where: In the running herd and mesquite thickets
scenes.weather: blinding sandstorm, pitch dark, keening wind
scenes.action: Blind and weeping mud, Newt clings low over the horn as Mouse runs among horned cattle and crashes through snapping mesquite limbs.

scenes.where: Among a few hundred slowed cattle
scenes.weather: lightning striking in thick bolts, thunder
scenes.action: In a flash Dish pulls on a yellow slicker; blue balls of light roll along the longhorns' horns and Deets looms up to order Newt away.
Water streams off Newt's hat brim front and back; a wet coyote darts past, and Mouse slides into a gully, then plods on through hock-deep water.

mentionedCharacters: a cowboy Dish knew who was turned black by lightning
visualDetails: The sun a dark disc with yellow edges behind the rising sand; evening star visible above
Sand rising like a brown curtain in the west and south; low sand streams weaving through mesquite and chaparral
Bolivar's serape
Newt's hat tied on with a rawhide string Deets fixed; Soupy's bandana over his nose
Dish's yellow slicker; Newt has no slicker
St Elmo's fire: little blue balls of lightning rolling along the cattle's horns
Clicking of long horns as cattle bump in the dark
Lightning in bolts thick as poles; wall of cloud to the west, clearing sky high to the east
A frightened wet coyote crossing in front of Mouse
Mouse's sides slick with sweat; one of Newt's boots full of water

locations: Jake and Lorena's camp under a big mesquite tree on the north bank of the Nueces River, South Texas (they crossed the Nueces in ch30)
Undercut riverbank of the Nueces a short way from the tree
Their earlier first camp, across the river (the tree there is struck)
events: Jake has forgotten to hobble the stock; at the first lightning Lorena's young mare snaps her rein and bolts into the dark, though Jake hobbles his own horse and the pack mule.
Lorena, rigid with terror of lightning, clings to the mesquite trunk while strikes hit the nearby trees.
Jake insists they get away from the tree; she fights him, punching him in the eye and kicking, until a very near strike stuns her into letting him drag her to the riverbank.
Huddled under the muddy tarp beneath the low bank, they watch a bolt split the tree at their old camp across the river.
Jake credits Deets's advice with saving them; Lorena silently notes he never actually thanked Deets.
season: Spring, early in the drive (the text elsewhere calls it a rainy spring; no month given). Inferred from the continuing storm sequence begun in ch31. Same night as ch31's storm.
herdPosition: Herd is still south of the Nueces in brush country, near Jake and Lorena's crossing (not stated in this chapter; inferred from ch30-35).
notes: The river is not named in this chapter; identified as the Nueces from ch30 (Lorena's first wash was in the Nueces) and ch34-35 (Gus swims the same muddy river back to the herd, which then crosses the Nueces). Jake tells Lorena he expects the mare will be found on their side of the river. Lorena wonders where 'the turtle' is, a callback to an earlier chapter. Deets had evidently warned Jake about sheltering under trees (Jake says so). Study guides agree.

scenes.where: Under a big mesquite tree at the riverside camp
scenes.weather: dark, sand still blowing, then lightning and rain
scenes.action: Lorena's mare breaks her rein and gallops off as the first lightning strikes while Jake fumbles hobbles onto his horse and the mule.

scenes.weather: constant lightning, heavy rain; a too-small tarp
scenes.action: In a glare of lightning Jake tugs Lorena from the tree; she slugs him and he sits down hard in the mud.

scenes.where: Under a low cutbank of the Nueces
scenes.weather: lightning so bright every wavelet shows; rain
scenes.action: The two shiver under a mud-caked tarp at the water's edge while the hobbled horses jump and fight their hobbles in the flashes.

scenes.where: Across the river, their first campsite
scenes.action: A bolt cracks into the tree at their old camp, splitting its top, which falls to the ground by the next flash.

visualDetails: Lorena's young mare (colour not stated) runs off; Jake's horse and a pack mule are hobbled
Lorena huddles in a blanket, back against a big mesquite, legs half buried in drifted sand, teeth clenched
Lightning shows every whisker on Jake's face; he looks old to her
A small tarp Jake tried to rig as a shelter, too small; later dragged, heavy with mud
The riverbank has only a slight overhang
Lorena's tears mix with the rain

locations: The Hat Creek cow camp and wagon in the wet mesquite and chaparral thickets south of the Nueces River, South Texas
A gully where the wagon is stuck
events: At a cloudless dawn Call finds the outfit came through the storm with few losses; the wagon is roped out of a gully.
Deets reports all hands safe except Gus, who was last seen riding east; Call sends Deets to look, wanting to cross the river soon.
Dish gloats over his night's work and his dry spare clothes while the crew strip and hang shirts on the bushes; Sean is revealed to have spent the night in the wagon after being bucked off.
The men argue over how many rivers lie between them and the Yellowstone.
Needle arms himself against the Texas bull, which stands watching the pigs root under a chaparral bush.
season: Spring, early in the drive (the text elsewhere calls it a rainy spring; no month given). Inferred from the continuing storm sequence begun in ch31. Morning after the storm.
herdPosition: South of the Nueces (the river is called 'just a creek' by Dish); main bunch plus a remnant a mile or two east held by Soupy, Jasper and Needle. Dish estimates at most 25 head lost.
notes: River is not named here but is the Nueces (crossed in ch35). Sean could not rope; Bill Spettle roped him an unrideable horse and it bucked him off and ran with the remuda. TheBestNotes wrongly gives Dish the line about not getting too dry; in the text it is Pea Eye. TheBestNotes also calls the Texas bull 'multi-colored', which is not stated here.

scenes.where: Wet brush south of the river
scenes.weather: rain stopped, sky cloudless; sunlight on puddles
scenes.action: Sun sparkles on dripping thickets and hundreds of puddles as Call surveys the calm, tired herd and a half-asleep Newt finds himself at the drag.
Cowboys haul the stuck wagon out with ropes while Bol refuses to leave the seat and Lippy, who pushed, is mud to the lip.
Half-naked cowhands with brown faces and white bodies spread shirts on bushes while Dish struts in dry clothes and the Raineys sleep under the wagon.
The Texas bull watches the pigs root at a chaparral bush; Needle props his rifle against a wagon wheel as he eats.

visualDetails: Most hands are burned deep brown on face, neck and hands but stark white elsewhere
Bert Borum: round fat belly with curly black hair
Pea Eye in all-enveloping long johns worn for years, with knife and gun belt buckled over them
Dish had his spare clothes wrapped in oilcloth
Bol keeps dry wood under a tarp
Newt dozes upright in the saddle; Mouse at a slow walk
Needle carries his rifle from his saddle scabbard

locations: Jake and Lorena's muddy camp on the north bank of the Nueces River, brushy country, South Texas
events: Lorena dries their soaked gear in the sun; the flour and salt are ruined but bacon and coffee survive, and Jake rides off downriver to find the mare.
Gus rides in leading the mare, eats bacon Lorena fries, admires how fresh and relaxed she looks, and fires two shots to call Jake back.
Jake wants to stop in San Antonio to gamble; Lorena twice refuses, and Jake slaps her in front of Gus.
Lorena ignores the slap and packs; Gus teases Jake, warns him lawmen may look for him in San Antonio, and tells Lorena to come find the herd by its dust if Jake leaves her.
Gus swims his horse back across the muddy river; Lorena, cheerful despite Jake's sulking, looks forward to the trip.
season: Spring, early in the drive (the text elsewhere calls it a rainy spring; no month given). Inferred from the continuing storm sequence begun in ch31. Morning after the storm (same morning as ch33).
herdPosition: South of the Nueces, not yet crossed (Gus swims back to it).
notes: River unnamed in chapter; Nueces inferred from ch30/35. Lorena remembers the money Xavier gave her. Jake mentions heading toward Denver. GradeSaver says Gus informs Jake he would take Jake's place with Lorena; broadly correct (he jokes he would camp with her). Study guides agree otherwise.

scenes.weather: sunny, clear blue sky, growing hot
scenes.action: Lorena drapes wet clothes over trees and bushes, washes mud off her legs in the river and naps on a grassy patch under the open sky.
Gus arrives with the runaway mare, slices bacon with his big clasp knife and fires his pistol into the air.
Jake gallops in, rifle in hand; when Lorena refuses San Antonio he wheels and slaps her.
Gus swims the muddy river, waves from the far bank and vanishes into the brush as Lorena finishes packing the mule.

mentionedCharacters: Benny Johnson (the dentist Jake shot, alluded to)
visualDetails: Lorena's hair not yet dry, the wet ends dark; water trickling down her bare arm; face relaxed and girlish
Gus's big clasp knife and his pistol
Gus flings coffee dregs into a chaparral bush
Gus calls the mare a fifty-dollar horse; he found her heading back toward Lonesome Dove
Jake gallops into camp holding his rifle
Pack mule loaded by Lorena

locations: Mesquite and chaparral brush country approaching the Nueces River, South Texas
A tall-grass clearing a mile or more wide just south of the river
The Nueces crossing (Deets's chosen crossing, slightly downriver)
Sean O'Brien's grave beside a live oak about 100 yards back from the north bank
Memory: in front of Clara's little store in Austin, Texas
Memory: a drying lake far up the Brazos River
events: Call pushes the tired herd through the brush to cross the Nueces before an expected storm; swarms of mosquitoes torment men and animals and a contrary red cow plagues Newt.
Dish eases Old Dog, a lead steer bought from the Pumphreys, to the front; Gus, seeing Dish's longing for Lorena, remembers losing Clara and muses about stopping at Ogallala.
The crossing goes smoothly until Sean rides into a nest of water moccasins; Pea Eye, Call, Gus and Deets charge in, Gus shoots snakes, and Pea drags Sean out.
Sean dies on the bank with many bites; Allen blames himself, and the rest of the crew, terrified, cross with the wagon.
Deets and Pea bury Sean under a live oak; Allen breaks down singing an Irish song, Gus speaks a few words, and the outfit rides on.
season: Spring, early in the drive (the text elsewhere calls it a rainy spring; no month given). Inferred from the continuing storm sequence begun in ch31. Day after the storm; Deets predicts another storm that night.
herdPosition: Crosses the Nueces River (first river of the drive); next river is the San Antonio.
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: Old Dog; also first naming of Dish's horse Mustache in the book. Gus has crossed the Nueces 'a hundred times' and never seen such a nest; Deets blames the storm and feels guilty for choosing the crossing. Clara memory: roughly sixteen years ago; she asked Gus to stay away ten years then visit. Dish wishes they were up to the Red River; Gus mentions the Yellowstone and Nebraska/Ogallala. Old Dog had led herds to Matagorda Bay. Newt wishes Sean had gone to Galveston for a boat. TheBestNotes says Newt reminds Gus of Clara (it is Dish) and says 'tall oak' (text: live oak). Allen sings an Irish song; no lyrics given.

scenes.action: Newt, smeared with blood from crushed mosquitoes, forces his horse into thicket after thicket to pop out a red cow.

scenes.weather: hot, clear; storm expected that night
scenes.action: Dish on his sorrel practice-ropes a mesquite seedling and a buzzard lifting off a dead armadillo while Gus recalls Clara (memory of her taking his hand before her Austin store).
Sean screams, writhing brown moccasins all over him and his horse, as riders lash with coiled ropes and Gus's Colt cracks at the snakes.
Sean lies dying on Call's slicker; Newt, holding cattle, weeps and vomits beside Mouse's neck.

scenes.where: Grave under a live oak 100 yards from the river
scenes.action: Sean, wrapped in a piece of wagon sheet, is buried; the men mount and ride off looking back through tall gray grass.

mentionedCharacters: Bob, the Kentucky horse trader Clara married
visualDetails: FIRST APPEARANCE: Old Dog, a big docile longhorn lead steer twice the size of the scrawny yearlings, with long, irregularly bent horns that look jointed
Dish's trim sorrel cow horse named Mustache, always watching for breakaway cattle
Gus rides old Malaria; carries a big Colt
Mosquitoes so thick on horses' withers they wipe off like stains; Sean's face lumpy with bites
Water moccasins: brown, like giant wiggling worms; Sean's horse shakes three off, one slithering off its neck
Eight sets of fang marks on Sean, one on the neck; his shirt cut off
Call's slicker laid under the dying boy; Gus's slicker used to cover the corpse
Allen O'Brien has a round face; stands crying over the grave
Horse herd comes up the bank and shakes spray over Deets
Bol sits grim on the wagon seat, feet barely wet as the wagon floats across

locations: A whiskey traders' boat moving up the Arkansas River westward from Fort Smith, Arkansas, out of the woods onto the open plains (Indian Territory/Kansas direction implied)
events: Elmira rides the stinking whiskey boat up the Arkansas, living in a cubbyhole among the casks, surprised the rough men leave her alone.
She thinks of July's shyness, her indifference to her son Joe, and her hope of finding Dee.
The river narrows onto the plains; she watches misty dawns, cranes, ducks and a huge full moon.
The morning after the full moon, Big Zwey kills a red-haired trader in a fight; the men strip the body and throw it overboard.
Fowler tells her the fight was over her and that Zwey wants to marry her; she resents being treated as his property and falls silent.
season: Spring: the banks are green with spring grass. A full moon occurs during the voyage. Time since leaving Fort Smith unstated (several days to weeks).
herdPosition: not stated in chapter
notes: The text names the chief trader 'Bowler' once and then 'Fowler' throughout (apparent typo in the edition); 'Fowler' is used in later chapters. The edition also misprints 'Port Smith' once for Fort Smith. Exact stretch of the Arkansas is not named; the text says the river winds out of the trees onto the plains. Elmira has been in Kansas before (a rescued Indian captive was pointed out to her there). Joe is twelve. Shmoop says Big Zwey threw the man overboard; the text says Fowler and a couple of men did it after Zwey killed him. TheBestNotes says two whiskey traders fought; text says a trader and a buffalo hunter.

scenes.where: Stern of the whiskey boat on the Arkansas
scenes.weather: some days shimmering hot, others chill rain
scenes.action: Elmira, wrapped in a buffalo robe, watches the brown water while Fowler, rifle in the crook of his arm, scans the banks for Indians.

scenes.where: Stern of the boat on the plains stretch
scenes.weather: mist frosting the river, clearing to blue sky
scenes.action: Ducks and geese burst out of the mist near her and a huge gray crane beats low over the boat.
A giant full moon seems to rise out of the smoky river, turning the mist pearl-colored before climbing, yellow as a melon.
Men strip the red-haired dead man of boots, belt and pockets and heave him over; his body bumps the boat and drifts into the mist.
Fowler brings her breakfast and explains the killing; from far down the boat Big Zwey sits staring at her for hours.

visualDetails: Cubbyhole among whiskey casks, roofed with planks and buffalo skins; fleas
Fowler: burly, dirty yellow beard, one eyelid that twitches and droops; chews and spits tobacco; always drinking; heavy rifle
Buffalo hunters: big men in buffalo-skin coats with long shaggy hair
Big Zwey: oily beard, fingernails black as tar
Dead trader identifiable by red hair; front of body stiff with blood
Banks green with spring grass; deer, coyotes, cattle, a gray wolf; hunters' bullets kick up mud
Gray cranes standing in the shallows beside strings of ducks
Stars by the millions; moon so large it seems to touch both banks

locations: Pine woods along the Army trail between Fort Smith, Arkansas and Texas
A small boggy creek
Roscoe's first camp about ten miles from Fort Smith
Louisa Brooks's stump-filled field, cabin and rail corral in the Arkansas woods near the trail, west of Fort Smith
characters: a pack of wild pigs led by a brown boar
events: Hours out of Fort Smith, wild pigs stampede Memphis; later the horse bogs in a creek and Roscoe loses a boot in the mud and sleeps sitting up in terror.
Following the Army trail, Roscoe finds a big woman in men's clothes, Louisa Brooks, pulling stumps with mules; she puts him to work and a lashing root knocks him flat.
Over a supper of nothing but corn bread she proposes marriage; he refuses and beds down behind the cabin, fearing her pet rattler Ed.
At sunup Louisa straddles and seduces the half-asleep Roscoe in the weeds while chickens watch.
Torn, Roscoe keeps his duty to July, says he may stop back, and rides west with mixed feelings as Louisa hitches her mules to another stump.
season: Not stated; hot and sultry nights suggest late spring/early summer. Roscoe left Fort Smith only the day before meeting Louisa.
herdPosition: not stated in chapter
notes: Roscoe rides west on the Army trail from Fort Smith toward Texas. Louisa is from Alabama, has buried three husbands and had eight children, and owns a section of land. The sexual scene should be handled discreetly in visuals. GradeSaver typo 'mills' for mules. Shmoop says he slept in the barn; text says outside against the back wall of the cabin. TheBestNotes says spring water; text says well water. FIRST APPEARANCE: Louisa Brooks and Ed the rattler.

scenes.where: Open pine woods near Fort Smith
scenes.action: A swift brown boar leads a pig pack after the fleeing white horse as Roscoe empties his pistol and drops his bullets.
Memphis bogs to the knees; Roscoe whips him out with a lariat and loses a boot deep in the mud.
Roscoe hacks roots with an ax as the mules strain; a freed root whips out like a snake and knocks him on his back.
By a small coal-oil lamp with bugs circling, Louisa eats corn bread from the pan and proposes marriage.

scenes.where: Behind the cabin in wet grass
scenes.weather: sultry, humid, mist; sun breaks through
scenes.action: Barefoot Louisa, feet wet with dew, sits astride the startled Roscoe as a few chickens look on and Ed crawls over a nearby log.

visualDetails: Memphis: a white, tallish horse, lazy, afraid of pigs
Louisa: large, fair-looking, brown hair, men's clothes and floppy hat, shirt sweated through; later a dress, men's brogans on bare feet, sunbonnet
Forty or fifty pulled stumps lined up at the south edge of the field
Large clean roomy cabin, rail corral, well water, chickens scratching; no pigs, no milk cow
Ed: a big rattlesnake that lives behind the cabin
Roscoe: 48, skinny, mustache, sleeps in long johns; bedroll tarp flops on Memphis's flank
Louisa's husband Jim buried right behind the house

locations: Rain-soaked pine woods southwest of Fort Smith, Arkansas
Scattered farms along the way
The Red River crossing (boggy, reddish sandbars), Texas–Indian Territory/Arkansas border, just before entering Texas
characters: a farmer's wife and her giggling little girls
events: July, sick with a nameless worry about Elmira, barely speaks and drives Joe and the horses sixteen hours a day, even riding on moonlit nights.
Farmers tell July that Jake Spoon spent the night with them; at one farm a wife gives them buttermilk.
At the Red River they find a tall stranger bogged midstream between a gaunt horse and a pack mule, calmly throwing his baggage into the water.
July and Joe cross at a deer ford and rope him out; he introduces himself as Sedgwick, a bug collector turned would-be preacher.
Sedgwick offers to take Joe and tells July he carries a heavy heart, unsettling him.
season: Spring (the text says it had been a rainy spring). About a week or more after leaving Fort Smith ('the first week of the trip' of silence).
herdPosition: not stated in chapter
notes: July names the river 'the Red' on sight, meaning they are about to reach Texas. Sedgwick says he left about a thousand bugs in Little Rock. FIRST APPEARANCE: Sedgwick (only appearance per file search). July's jaundice is referenced in other chapters, not here. Shmoop wrongly calls Joe the sulky silent one; it is July. TheBestNotes says Joe was unnerved by Sedgwick's insight; the text gives that reaction to July.

scenes.weather: rainy spring, dripping trees, puddles, mosquitoes
scenes.action: July and Joe slog southwest in silence; Joe dozes in the saddle, bumpy with mosquito bites.
A farmer's wife hands out glasses of buttermilk while little girls giggle at Joe.
A man in a tall beaver hat and frock coat stands knee-deep in the shallow muddy river tossing parcels and his bedroll downstream.
July flings two knotted ropes and drags the horse and mule free; Sedgwick wades out and later wanders off peering at the ground.

visualDetails: Red River: broad, muddy, shallow, boggy, curving down from the north; reddish bar of earth
Sedgwick: tall, blue eyes, tall beaver hat, long frock coat, sidearm under the coat
Sedgwick's gaunt horse and little brown pack mule, both sunk past the hocks
Parcels float away or lie in shallow water
July wears his badge; the two tie their ropes together
Water at the deer and cattle ford seldom over a foot deep

locations: Brushy South Texas trail between the Nueces and the San Antonio River
A shallow crossing of the San Antonio River a mile or two from camp, found by Deets
events: For a week the camp talks of nothing but Sean's death; Jasper chatters from fear while Allen rides silent and weeps by the fire.
Rain, mosquitoes and brush fray tempers: Bert and Soupy nearly fight, Bol resents Lippy's firewood, Deets is gloomy, the Raineys are homesick, but Dish proves a superb point man.
Deets finds a shallow San Antonio crossing; Call and Gus scout it for snakes and argue whether talking about the death helps.

The crossing goes well except Jasper charging the river at a gallop and nearly falling; Gus tells Newt he doubts he himself will make it if luck turns bad, then delights in the blue pigs swimming the river.
season: Spring, early in the drive (the text elsewhere calls it a rainy spring; no month given). Inferred from the continuing storm sequence begun in ch31. About a week after Sean's death; three days of rain.
herdPosition: Crosses the San Antonio River (second named river after the Nueces), south/southeast of the town of San Antonio.
notes: The men speculate how far north moccasins live, naming the Cimarron, Arkansas and Platte rivers. Pea Eye's recurring dream of a big Indian begins to trouble him again after leaving Lonesome Dove. Call voices the purpose of the drive: get the land in Montana before settlers arrive. TheBestNotes says Allen 'weeps silently' and that the crossing was narrow; text says shallow. GradeSaver says Allen 'ceases speaking altogether' (text: rides in silence).

scenes.action: Cowboys trade stories of deaths around the fire while Allen O'Brien sits crying.

scenes.where: Bank of the San Antonio River
scenes.action: Gus in his big yellow slicker and Call sit their horses on the bank scanning for snakes as the herd appears, the Texas bull walking beside Old Dog.
Jasper gallops his horse into the river and it stumbles; Soupy laughs.
The wagon rolls through with Lippy in back, followed by the remuda, and the two blue pigs wade in and swim across.

visualDetails: Gus wears a big yellow slicker
The Texas bull sometimes leads alongside Old Dog
Blue pigs wallow in puddles and root rats from holes, then swim the river
Deets reports only a few turtles at the crossing
Dish holds point 'true as a rule'

locations: A small clearing camp about an hour's ride from San Antonio, Texas, about a mile from the Hat Creek herd
events: Lorena grows to love travel despite nightly thunderstorms; Deets, who checks on them almost daily, has taught her to build fires and pack the mule.
Jake sulks over San Antonio, calls her a whore, threatens her, and rides off to town.
Alone at dusk she enjoys the night, hears the Irishman singing to the herd, then Jake gallops back drunk hoping to catch her with another man.
Drunk, Jake takes her, then broods about ditching her in Austin, predicts he will be hanged, and tells her Call once kept a whore, Maggie, Newt's mother.
season: Spring, early in the drive (the text elsewhere calls it a rainy spring; no month given). Inferred from the continuing storm sequence begun in ch31. A few days after the Nueces crossing; herd near San Antonio.
herdPosition: About a mile from Jake's camp, near San Antonio (an hour's ride), after the San Antonio River crossing; Austin said to be two days away.
notes: The singer is called 'the Irishman' (Allen O'Brien). Jake says a fortune-teller predicted he would hang, and that he and Gus both knew Maggie; Jake had 'sported' with Elmira in Kansas. Jake mentions a thorn he'd had in his hand (earlier chapter). GradeSaver says Deets visits nearly every night; the text says almost every day.

scenes.action: Lorena sits on damp blankets feeling the sun warm her slowly tanning arms.
At the campfire Jake rages that she won't talk, threatens her with a rope and rides off into the dusk.
Bullbats swoop as dark shapes overhead and a possum waddles within ten feet of Lorena sipping coffee; faint singing drifts from the herd.
Jake gallops in raising dust over the blankets, whiskey bottle half empty, and later talks of hangings and Maggie under the stars.

mentionedCharacters: Allen O'Brien (heard singing to the herd)
visualDetails: Nightly lightning and big raindrops; a hot stiff tarp; permanently damp blankets
Lorena's arms slowly tanning; her mare no longer looks back toward Lonesome Dove
Bullbats (nighthawks) whooshing at dusk; a possum
Jake's half-empty whiskey bottle

locations: A little creek with a three-foot cutbank, on the trail near (south of) San Antonio, Texas
Bolivar's ride south toward the Rio Grande ('the river'), Lonesome Dove and his village in Mexico
events: Before the herd passes San Antonio, the wagon mules bolt; Jim Rainey's attempt to head them sends the wagon off a cutbank and it flips onto Lippy, whose coat is pinched in the seat.
Gus ropes a wheel from Malaria to tilt the wagon, Newt and the Raineys hold Lippy's head up, and Pea cuts the coat with his bowie knife; Lippy revives, belching water.
The rotten wagon bed has burst and the supplies float; Bol walks up with the pigs and resigns, secretly because he fired his ten-gauge while dreaming and spooked the mules.
Call gives Bol a gentle gelding; Bol rides south bareback on a serape, regretting his choice but planning to beat the old dinner bell in Lonesome Dove, while Newt grieves another loss.
season: Spring, early in the drive (the text elsewhere calls it a rainy spring; no month given). Inferred from the continuing storm sequence begun in ch31. Bol reckons a week has passed since leaving Lonesome Dove.
herdPosition: Just past a little creek near San Antonio, after the San Antonio River crossing; herd has not yet passed the town.
notes: The creek is unnamed. Bol has cooked for them ten years and has never been more than two days' ride from the border. The dinner bell and crowbar recur here (not first appearance). Bill Spettle says the shot sounded like a shotgun. TheBestNotes says Bol held a 'rifle' and dreamed of wife and daughters; text: ten-gauge, dreaming of daughters, then of his angry wife.

scenes.action: The driverless wagon races toward the creek with Lippy frozen on the seat, and plunges off a three-foot bank, flipping with all four wheels spinning.
Gus on Malaria ropes a spinning wheel to tip the wagon while the boys lift Lippy's mud-covered head from the water.
Lippy rolls over belching water as cowboys fish bedrolls out of the shallows and a flour sack sits ruining in the river.
Bol walks up carrying his gun with the pigs at his side, resigns, and rides off south on a gentle gelding, his old gun across its withers.
(memory) Bol beats the dinner bell with the broken crowbar and listens to the echoes fade into Mexico.

events: Lost among settlers who can't direct him, Roscoe joins four drunk soldiers heading to Buffalo Springs, gets violently sick in their springless wagon, and is heaved onto Memphis at the Red River.
The soldiers point him southwest toward San Antonio; at dusk he stops at a cabin where a hostile old man, Sam, skins a possum and claims the girl inside as bought property.
Sam drinks Roscoe's whiskey and gives him no supper; in the night Roscoe hears him beat and force the girl but does not intervene.
Next day a wasp nest drops into Roscoe's lap; the girl, Janey, who has followed on foot, packs his stings with mud, kills a rabbit and a bullfrog and cooks them.
Janey says she crippled Sam's knees with a pan; Roscoe lets her ride double for a day or two to guide him toward San Antonio.
season: Not stated; hot days and heavy dew. Some days to weeks after Roscoe left Fort Smith.
herdPosition: not stated in chapter
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: Janey. The text does not say whether Sam's cabin is north or south of the Red; Roscoe calls Sam the first person he saw in Texas, so it is south of the river. Buffalo Springs is named as the soldiers' Texas destination. Janey came from San Antonio and was being taken to Fort Worth by Bill until traded to Sam 'up there by Waco' (the geography is loose; Waco is well south of the Red). 'The Territory' (Indian Territory) lies west. The chapter contains period racial language; do not reproduce. GradeSaver says Roscoe lets Janey come to San Antonio; the text says only for a day or two while he decides.

A wasp nest falls in Roscoe's lap; after loping clear he strips off his shirt and spots the girl ducking behind a bush.
Janey smacks a leaping bullfrog with a stick, fries rabbit and frog legs, and gray turtles gather to nibble scraps in the creek.

locations: Jake and Lorena's camp by a cold pool at the foot of a limestone bluff, rolling plain to the west, west of Austin, Texas
events: Lorena, discouraged after two days alone, has thought of drowning herself but only washes her hair; Gus talks to her about hope and holds her hand.
Gus strips to his worn underwear, swims the cold pool, then from a rock spots a rider far off on a pacing horse and asks for his gun belt.
A big Indian on a bay stallion with a silver-trimmed saddle rides in, waters, and names himself Blue Duck; he says he'd been told to kill both Rangers, trades threats with Gus, and rides off.
Gus explains Blue Duck is a Comanchero raider; Lorena refuses to go to the cow camp and waits for Jake.
Lorena asks Gus to take her to California; he says he's bound for Ogallala and Clara, offers a train ticket from Denver, and leaves; she stays angry.

Lorena weeps as Gus wipes her tears, then sits silent and angry on the rock as he rides away.

Her mare and then the pack-horse give out; she rides double behind him and then bareback on a stolen horse, noticing his necklace of human finger bones.

events: At dawn July and Joe hear and then see a huge trail herd moving north across the misty plain.
At the wagon they meet the boss, Wilbarger, reading Milton; he says Jake Spoon was in Lonesome Dove and is coming north with the Rangers who got his horses back.
Wilbarger offers Joe a job, which Joe declines out of duty to July.
July rides a few miles with Wilbarger toward the Red River, then turns back east toward Arkansas to look for Roscoe, leaving Joe privately frustrated.
season: Wilbarger says 'it's summertime'. This conflicts with ch54 and ch58, which call it spring; treat as late spring/early summer.
herdPosition: Hat Creek herd not present; Wilbarger's (a different outfit's) herd is in north Texas heading for the Red River. Wilbarger estimates the Hat Creek outfit is two or three weeks behind.
notes: Exact spot not named: it is the camp July made a few hours' ride east of Fort Worth at the end of ch50, so somewhere in north Texas between Fort Worth and the Red River road. Wilbarger (first seen in Part I buying horses) reappears. Wilbarger mistakenly says July overshot Jake, who is 'headed this way'. July's direction at the end is east, back toward Arkansas. Season discrepancy noted above. GradeSaver says July offered to 'test the freshness' of the Red River - July only asked to ride along.

events: Janey guides Roscoe west along the trail on foot, catching rabbits, squirrels and a prairie chicken, and hiding from strangers.
Two outlaws, Jim and Hutto, follow and cut them off; Janey takes Roscoe's pistol, a thunderstorm breaks, and the outlaws capture her and strip Roscoe naked hunting for money.
Janey slips her bonds and pelts the outlaws with rocks until July, drawn by the gunfire, steps in and arrests them.
They ride all night to Fort Worth to hand over the prisoners; July learns from Roscoe only that Elmira left, and pays a livery woman to board Janey.
Janey follows them anyway and turns up at their camp twenty miles north of town, returning July's money.

notes: Exact spot of the robbery unnamed; Hutto says they are not far from 'the Territory' (Indian Territory), yet July reaches Fort Worth after one night's ride, so it is somewhere on the Fort Smith-to-Texas road within a night of Fort Worth. GradeSaver says Roscoe 'calls Janey to join them' successfully and that July 'arms her' - she ignored the call and only appeared later; July handed her the shotgun just to hold. GradeSaver's 'family of 16' fits (14 children plus parents).

Through Fowler, Big Zwey proposes; after Zwey bolts in embarrassment when she surprises him at her door, Elmira agrees to go with him if he takes her to Ogallala.
Zwey has a hide wagon patched and buys mules; his partner Luke joins, and Elmira drives the wagon north while the men hunt buffalo.
A night thunderstorm drives her under the wagon; she resolves to get used to hard travel.

Mentioned: Staked Plains, Adobe Walls (the Bents' abandoned fort on the Canadian), the Valley of Tears, the Comanchero captive-trading crossing on the Canadian, Blanco country, San Antonio, Waco, the Trinity, the Pecos, Lonesome Dove, Montana
events: Gus spends half a day finding Blue Duck's tracks, which were hidden in the stampede, then follows them northwest, recalling his rusty tracking and an old hanging.
He crosses the Clear Fork of the Brazos, finds Lorena's dead mare, crosses the Wichita and gambles that Blue Duck is heading for the country north and west of Palo Duro.
He crosses the Quitaque and the Prairie Dog Fork to the edge of the Palo Duro, passing bleached bone fields, and reaches the Canadian breaks without finding Blue Duck's track.
He meets Aus Frank, an old outlaw he once arrested, wheeling buffalo bones to giant pyramids by the Canadian; Aus says Blue Duck runs with six Kiowas who ate his dog.
At dawn Gus rides east along a road of buffalo bones toward Adobe Walls, musing on the emptied plains.
season: Stated: 'It was spring' (Gus reasons the remaining buffalo would be moving north).
herdPosition: Herd left behind west of Austin; not otherwise stated.
notes: Richest geography chapter in this range. Route order as given: Clear Fork of the Brazos, Brazos post-oak country, mare carcass, Wichita, Quitaque, Prairie Dog Fork of the Red, west edge of Palo Duro, spring, Canadian breaks, then east along the Canadian. The Red River proper is not named in this chapter (ch56 says Blue Duck crossed the Red and went straight north, so Gus's westward swing was a wrong guess). FIRST APPEARANCE: Aus Frank. Memory scenes: hanging Webster Witter from a sagging mesquite in the Blanco country; a two-hour gunfight with Aus Frank in a Brazos thicket near Waco; Call and Gus turning back at the western edge of Palo Duro in midsummer. GradeSaver says Blue Duck 'always retreated to the Palo Duro Canyon' - text says an area north and west of it. Gus's own horse is not named in this chapter (it is Jerry from ch48).

Half-built abandoned cabin on the Clear Fork of the Brazos.
Memory: the Rangers once rode alongside the vast southern buffalo herd for nearly a hundred miles.

Quitaque (mentioned by Blue Duck as where Gus went astray)

Lorena has gone mute from terror; the Kiowas kill a crippled cow and eat its raw guts.
Blue Duck brings whiskey, wins all the men's horses at dice, and shoots the young Kiowa who refuses to wager his share of Lorena.
Having won Lorena outright, Blue Duck returns her and the horses in exchange for killing the old Ranger coming down the river.
At dawn the Kiowas ride out with Blue Duck's bullets to kill Gus; Blue Duck leaves, and Monkey John, clubbed by Dog Face overnight, wakes half-blind from ant stings.

Mentioned: the Red River, Lonesome Dove, Kansas, Arkansas, Fort Smith

a white buffalo hunter with a .50-caliber gun on a tripod
events: Riding east on the plain south of the Canadian, Gus is ambushed by about a dozen Indians and cannot outrun them.
In a shallow buffalo wallow he cuts his own horse's throat so the blood spooks their mounts, and kills six, including a leader who charges with his horse blindfolded.
A buffalo hunter with a tripod-mounted .50-caliber pins him down until dark; then shots to the east drive the attackers off.
Carrying his saddle, Gus walks into the camp of July Johnson, Roscoe, Joe and Janey; he gives Joe a captured Winchester and they ride to the Canadian and spot a campfire downriver.
Leaving the others at a canyon mouth a mile upriver, Gus and July ride on Roscoe's gelding and July's horse toward the fire, Gus uneasy that July has never killed.
season: Not stated here; spring per ch54 and ch58.
herdPosition: Not relevant.
notes: Gus confirms Blue Duck crossed the Red and went straight north, whereas Gus had swung west - key for the route map. The wallow is roughly ten miles south of the Canadian, east of Aus Frank's camp; July's party camp is at the mouth of a canyon on the Canadian, a mile upriver of where they first saw Blue Duck's fire, and the raid ride covers seven or eight miles east. The horse Gus kills is his only horse, i.e. Jerry the sorrel from ch48 (not named here). Blue Duck's attackers are described only as Indians (ch57 names Ermoke among the dead). Shmoop says some attackers were white men; in the text they are Indians, with one white buffalo hunter fetched later. Gus's 'practically in Kansas' is banter, not geography. Gus asks July about his brother; July calls Jake's shooting of his brother likely accidental.

The river, toward which Blue Duck rides away

Gus and July charge the camp at a run; Gus shoots Monkey John and kills every Kiowa, riding down the one who flees, and finishes Monkey John when he fires at July.

Mentioned: Adobe Walls (not far down the river), the Purgatory (Purgatoire) River in Colorado, the Arkansas, Kansas, Fort Smith/Arkansas, Tennessee
characters: Blue Duck (seen only as a big shadow)
events: Left without a fire at the canyon camp, Roscoe, Joe and Janey wait nervously; Janey runs off to check a suspected Indian that turns out to be a bush.
Roscoe dozes and wakes to Janey hurling a rock at a big shadowy man, who stabs Roscoe and strikes Janey down as she crawls for the pistol; Joe is already dead.
July returns an hour later to find all three dead, and digs shallow graves with his knife until sunup.
Gus arrives with Lorena, wraps the mutilated bodies in blankets, buries them under rocks, and deduces Blue Duck took Joe's horse and is likely heading for the Purgatory.
Gus talks July out of revenge; July rides north across the river to seek Elmira, and Gus leads the silent Lorena east to wait for Call's herd.

Buried on the plain above the canyon. Gus names the Purgatory River in Colorado as Blue Duck's likely destination. July crosses the Canadian northward toward Kansas; Gus steers him away from Adobe Walls. Gus recalls he could have been a lawyer in Tennessee. Shmoop says Gus buried the bodies 'so July can rest' - July keeps digging and both pile rocks. Graphic wounds summarized. Gus mentions Call and the boys will come with the cattle 'pretty soon', though he plans to wait a couple of weeks.

Fort Worth, Texas (the hands go into town off-page)
