events: Days and then a week pass with no sign of Gus while the herd crosses the Brazos and the Trinity uneventfully.
Call camps the herd west of Fort Worth and lets most of the men go to town, keeping only the boys; Dish stays behind, still pining for Lorena.
Po Campo, whittling by the wagon, reveals that Blue Duck killed his three sons on the llano and predicts Gus will not catch him on the horse he took.
Call grows increasingly convinced Gus may be dead and half-wishes he could abandon the herd to search for him.
The hands return hung over, report that Jake snubbed them while gambling with a whore in Fort Worth, and eat Po Campo's dewberry cobbler; Jasper straggles in last on foot.
season: Spring - the text mentions excellent spring grass; the drive is perhaps three to four weeks old (Gus has been gone over a week).
herdPosition: Brazos and Trinity crossed; herd camped west of Fort Worth, Texas; next river is the Red River.
notes: The herd does NOT enter Fort Worth; it is held west of the town and the hands ride in. Fort Worth is described as the last town they will see before Ogallala. Jake is reported (second-hand) to be gambling in Fort Worth. Po Campo's backstory: he once tried sheep ranching on the llano and Blue Duck killed his three sons. Deets is fascinated by the whittling. Allen O'Brien reminisces about hangovers in Ireland.

scenes.where: trail camp west of Fort Worth, men gathered in groups
scenes.action: The hands tease Dish for staying sober while the Texas bull paws and bellows fifty yards off; Dish jumps Jasper and Call breaks up the fight.

scenes.where: by the chuck wagon, Po Campo's back against a wheel
scenes.action: Po Campo, wood shavings over his short legs, whittles a tiny wooden woman while telling Call that Blue Duck killed his sons and always has the best horse.

scenes.where: riding ahead of the strung-out herd on the prairie
scenes.action: Call keeps looking northwest for Gus and broods that he might have died unseen on the llano.

scenes.where: trail from Fort Worth back to camp
scenes.action: Hung-over riders return and eat Po Campo's sugary dewberry cobbler while Jasper walks the last two miles, stopping to vomit.

mentionedCharacters: Po Campo's three sons (killed by Blue Duck)
visualDetails: Po Campo carves small female figures about two inches high from big chunks of wood he collects along the trail and tosses in the wagon.
Po Campo is short-legged and sits with his back to a wagon wheel covered in shavings.
The Texas bull resents cowboys sitting in groups: he stands about fifty yards away, pawing and bellowing.
Bert Borum is proud of his roping; he once roped a coyote on the first throw.
Po Campo's hangover cure: a dewberry cobbler, and a spoonful of molasses forced on Jasper.
Cattle are trail-broken; spring grass is excellent and water plentiful.
Call's mare (the Hell Bitch, unnamed here) is called the best horse in the country.

locations: treeless rolling plain south of the Red River, North Texas
Red River - the Texas/Indian Territory boundary; a better gravel-bar crossing found downstream of the first probe
north bank of the Red River, Oklahoma (Indian) Territory
Call's separate camp apart from the crew
Lonesome Dove (remembered by Newt)
the Red River 'over toward Arkansas' (Dish's memory of an earlier drive for Mr. Pierce)
events: Two days short of the Red River a black storm rolls in from the northwest and the crew endures a sodden night on horseback.
Dish confides in Newt that Jake is to blame for losing both Gus and Lorena and vows he will still marry her; Newt reluctantly revises his boyhood hero-worship of Jake.
At the Red, Call worries about quicksand in a hundred yards of rust-coloured sand; Deets probes, dislikes the crossing and finds a gravel bar downstream.
The sun breaks through as Old Dog leads the herd across into the Territory; a few bogged cows are roped out.
That night the Irishman and Po Campo sing; apart from the crew, Call catches himself talking aloud to the absent Gus while cleaning his rifle, the Hell Bitch tethered to his wrist.
season: Spring - morning described as springlike; weeks into the drive.
herdPosition: Crosses the Red River into the Oklahoma (Indian) Territory; next major river is the Canadian.
notes: Exact crossing point on the Red is not named (the text does not mention Doan's store). Dish recalls bogging sixty of Mr. Pierce's cattle in the Red further east toward Arkansas. The Hell Bitch is named in this chapter. Old Dog leads the crossing. Deets and Po Campo are the crew's weather experts.

scenes.where: treeless rolling plain two days south of the Red River
scenes.timeOfDay: morning into early afternoon, then night
scenes.weather: fair spring morning, then low black clouds from the northwest and two hours of torrential rain
scenes.action: Newt mopes along on Mouse in the downpour; that night everyone herds because a horse is drier than the soaked ground.

scenes.where: at the point of the herd
scenes.weather: iron-grey skies, rain pouring off hat brims
scenes.action: Dish, water streaming off his hat, tells Newt he still means to marry Lorena.

scenes.where: low banks of the Red River, wide stretch of wet rusty sand
scenes.weather: still raining, then rain slackens and sun breaks through
scenes.action: Deets vanishes downriver into the rain and returns with news of a gravel bar; Old Dog leads the herd across in sunshine while Dish and Soupy strip to wade in the mud and rope out bogged cows.

scenes.where: camp on the long wet grass north of the Red
scenes.action: The Irishman sings for hours and Po Campo sings sad Spanish songs, shaking a gourd rattle.

scenes.where: Call's solitary camp apart from the crew
scenes.action: Cleaning his rifle, Call startles himself by speaking aloud to Gus; the mare grazes at the end of a long rope looped to his belt and wrist.

mentionedCharacters: Mr. Pierce (Shanghai Pierce, Dish's former employer)
visualDetails: Rolling plain bare of trees; nothing to shelter under.
Red River: not wide or deep, but approached over more than a hundred yards of wet, rusty-coloured sand; the water is brownish; the Red is known for quicksand.
Deets waves the others back with his hat before loping downstream.
A gravel bar makes the river entrance almost like a road.
Five or six weak cows bog coming out; Dish and Soupy strip and wade in, Bert Borum hauls them out with ropes.
North bank: long wet grass of the Oklahoma Territory.
Po Campo has a gourd rattle, a low throaty voice, deep-set eyes, and a big-brimmed hat he rarely removes.
Deets keeps a whittled wooden woman from Po Campo in the pocket of his old chaps.
Call ties the Hell Bitch's long rope under his belt and around his wrist at night; she wakes him if she lifts her head at a deer or wolf.

locations: Adobe Walls - deserted, mostly ruined trading post/fort on the Texas Panhandle plains (site of the buffalo hunters' battle about two years earlier)
open prairie along the Canadian River, Texas Panhandle
ridge above the Canadian where four trail herds wait for the river to fall
Gus and Lorena's tent camp on a long ridge about two miles north of the Canadian River
San Francisco (Lorena's remembered goal)
Fort Worth, Denver, the Purgatory (Purgatoire) River, Ogallala (mentioned)
events: Caught by chill rains two days east of the buffalo hunters' camp, Gus shelters with Lorena for two days in a roofed room at deserted Adobe Walls.
Gus finds a woman's box of buttons, deals cards for button stakes, and Lorena speaks for the first time since her rescue.

Following the high Canadian, they find four herds waiting for the river to drop; Wilbarger rides out, feeds them, lends a tent and shares a bottle with Gus, and learns July Johnson's companions were killed by Blue Duck.
After the herds cross, Gus and Lorena cross the lowered Canadian and camp two miles north for about a week, playing cards as rain returns.
On an evening at the river Lorena bathes, is shocked at how pale her body is, and breaks down sobbing; Gus comforts her.
season: Spring rains; Gus notes the Adobe Walls fight was not two years earlier (the 1874 battle, so roughly spring 1876 by that reckoning, though the novel's dating is loose).
herdPosition: Hat Creek herd is behind, south of the Canadian (Wilbarger thought them three weeks behind him); Gus waits for it north of the Canadian.
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: the button box (Gus and Lorena's card stakes) and Wilbarger's borrowed tent. Adobe Walls is named explicitly. Gus says July was left four days earlier, headed north. Wilbarger's foreman died south of Fort Worth when a bronc fell backwards on him; Wilbarger asks for the tent to be returned in Denver. Gus's 'unfinished business in Ogallala' is Clara (inferred). Gus believes Blue Duck is heading for the Purgatory River. Study-guide check: GradeSaver compresses the Canadian episode as if Gus and Lorena leave the morning after meeting Wilbarger; the text has them cross the river after the herds and camp about a week on a ridge two miles north before the bath scene. TheBestNotes says Gus had once seen soldiers at Adobe Walls; the text only has him recall the fight and a woman who fled.

scenes.where: ruined Adobe Walls, a room with an intact roof
scenes.weather: chill steady rain; leak drips down one wall
scenes.action: Gus pokes an owl's nest from the fireplace, burns an old wagon, and they play cards on a blanket for buttons sorted by size.

scenes.where: outside the wagon yard at Adobe Walls
scenes.weather: rain stops an hour or two before dawn; bright sun on wet prairie
scenes.action: Gus shoots a grazing deer; that night Lorena wakes crying and he holds her, then at sunrise she weeps as they mount to leave.

scenes.where: ridge overlooking the Canadian River plain
scenes.action: Four great herds are spread across the plain; Wilbarger gallops out on the bay stolen back from Pedro Flores.

scenes.where: Gus's camp on the treeless plain near Wilbarger's herd
scenes.weather: fine sunny morning, plains dried out
scenes.action: Wilbarger brings beefsteak, beans, a tent and whiskey; Lorena watches through the tent flap; next morning the cook's mule nearly kicks him.

scenes.where: Canadian River bank near the ridge camp two miles north
scenes.action: Gus suns himself naked on a rock while Lorena, thigh-deep in the fast river, sees her white belly and brown legs and sobs uncontrollably.

mentionedCharacters: Clara (implied as the 'unfinished business in Ogallala')
visualDetails: Adobe Walls: deserted, buildings mostly in ruins, rattlesnakes, mice and owls; an owl's nest in the fireplace; a wagon yard.
Gus cuts Lorena a crude poncho from a tarp taken at the buffalo hunters' camp.
Box of assorted buttons; large horn coat buttons count as fifty-dollar gold pieces.
Lorena is thinner, cheeks hollowed, bruises healing; she wears a ragged dress.
Wilbarger rides a nice bay horse (formerly stolen from Pedro Flores).
Wilbarger's small pack mule, bad-tempered, carries a pot of beefsteak and beans and a small tent.
The plain around the Canadian is treeless.
Gus's improvised fishing line: coarse thread from Adobe Walls, a bent needle hook, tadpole bait; he catches nothing.
Gus's white hair; Gus strips to bathe whenever at the river.
Wilbarger also gives coffee and a side of bacon.

locations: empty grass plains of the Indian (Oklahoma) Territory between the Red and the Canadian
open plain half a day south of the Canadian River where lightning strikes the herd
the stampede ground, six or seven miles west of the main herd by dawn
Canadian River - a heavily used herd crossing about four miles from where the herd regrouped, twenty yards of swimming water, six-foot banks
north bank of the Canadian
Dodge City and Ogallala (mentioned in talk)
events: In the Territory the men fear Indians but see only empty grass and sky; Po Campo gives each cowboy a whittled woman.
Half a day from the Canadian a lightning storm strikes: a bolt kills thirteen cattle, the herd stampedes west, and the crew rides blind through a rainy night.
At dawn Dish brings word that lightning also killed Bill Spettle; he is buried hastily and the herd moves on without Newt seeing the grave.
Call pushes on to the Canadian; the men strip naked to swim the herd across, and a violent hailstorm with egg-sized stones pelts them mid-crossing.
After the hail, the men skip hailstones on the river, Po Campo gathers hail in a bucket, and Pea Eye spots Gus riding toward them.
season: Spring rains (not otherwise dated).
herdPosition: Crosses the Canadian River in the Indian Territory (Oklahoma); Red River is behind; Gus and Lorena are camped just north.
notes: Bill Spettle dies here (second boy lost after Sean O'Brien). Newt mistakes hail for his first sight of snow. The crossing point is described only as a heavily used herd crossing four miles from the regroup point; geographically this is in western Indian Territory, but the text does not name any town or landmark. Gus is seen 'across the river' riding toward them - slightly odd given his camp is north of the river; ch63 confirms he came to the north bank. The pigs appear (the blue shoat is specified in ch63).

scenes.weather: lightning flickering in the west all afternoon; a bolt runs south to north across the setting sun
scenes.action: A bolt seems to split the red setting sun, then black clouds roll down like a herd and snuff out the afterglow.

scenes.where: edge of the herd on the open plain
scenes.weather: constant thunder, lightning, then a wall of rain
scenes.action: Lightning drops a row of cattle like bricks a hundred feet from Call; the herd bolts west as bluish light rolls along the horn tips.

scenes.where: wet plain with a thousand strayed cattle
scenes.action: Dish returns with Deets and the news that Bill Spettle was struck dead and is being buried.

scenes.weather: chilly squall, then heavy hail growing to pullet-egg size
scenes.action: Naked riders swim the herd over as hail peppers the water; Newt crouches under Mouse, Jasper hides under his slicker and saddle, Pea Eye stands neck-deep in the river with his hat on.

scenes.where: hail-whitened north bank of the Canadian
scenes.weather: hail over within ten minutes; plains turned white
scenes.action: Men skip hailstones across the river, Po Campo fills a bucket with hail trailed by his two pigs, and a lone rider appears who Pea Eye knows is Gus.

visualDetails: Endless grass and sky; occasional wolves and coyotes; no trees.
Each cowboy now owns one of Po Campo's carved wooden women.
Thirteen cattle killed by one bolt; bluish St Elmo's-type light on the horn tips; clicking horns as the cattle run.
Bill Spettle was turned black by the lightning (reported); buried stiff, wrapped in a bedroll.
Pete Spettle holds the remuda together all night, looking weary and stunned.
Men ride naked across the Canadian, clothes and boots wrapped in slickers tied high on saddles; bodies fish-belly white except brown hands and faces; Deets is one colour.
Dish holds his saddle strings as his horse swims; mistakes the first hail for bullets.
Mouse jumps a six-foot bank into the river, throwing Newt.
Hailstones cover the muddy banks and plain; cattle and horses crunch through them.
Po Campo's two pigs follow him like dogs.

locations: north bank of the Canadian River, Indian (Oklahoma) Territory, covered in hailstones
Gus and Lorena's tent (Wilbarger's), visible at a distance from the crossing
Hat Creek camp near the Canadian
a spot a mile or two west of camp where Call camps alone
mentioned: Fort Worth, Colorado, the Purgatory River, Nebraska, Montana, the Powder River, the Nueces (Sean O'Brien's grave), China
events: Gus rides up on a different horse as Call and Dish dress, announcing he rescued Lorena and has waited north of the Canadian for a week.
The cheered crew swims back to bring the wagon over; the blue shoat jumps out and swims across on its own; Po Campo serves hailstones dipped in molasses.
Gus learns of Bill Spettle's death and tells Call about July's losses; Call condemns Jake as a coward and regrets that Blue Duck escaped.
A crippled steer is butchered for steaks while Lorena, hidden in the tent, keeps watch on Gus's white hair and relives Blue Duck's cruelty.
Riding out at dusk, Gus teases Call about Maggie and marriage and urges him to sell the herd and hunt Blue Duck; Call refuses, set on Montana, and camps alone under a thin moon.
season: Spring (continuing); Gus has been gone well over two weeks.
herdPosition: Just north of the Canadian River in Indian Territory; next stages lead toward Kansas.
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE (explicit): the blue shoat, one of the two pigs brought from Lonesome Dove. Gus reunites with the herd here. Gus implies he will pursue Clara ('someone else in mind'). Maggie (Newt's mother) raised by Gus. Call thinks Jake will never be part of the old crew again. Gus suggests Blue Duck is in Colorado up the Purgatory.

scenes.where: hail-strewn north bank of the Canadian
scenes.weather: sun comes out after the hail
scenes.action: Gus's horse crunches over hailstones as he rides up to half-dressed Call and Dish and jokes about naked cowboys.

scenes.where: Canadian River crossing and the dripping wagon
scenes.weather: bright sun, clouds only wisps on the eastern horizon
scenes.action: The blue shoat leaps from the wagon and swims the river; Po Campo hands out molasses-dipped hailstones, Lippy licking his on the wagon seat.
Lorena peeps out only to find Gus's white hair by the wagon, calming herself against memories of Blue Duck.
Bert ropes a steer crippled in the crossing, Po Campo kills it with an axe, and the famished men devour beefsteaks while Gus jokes.

scenes.where: a little way out of camp, then a mile or two west
scenes.weather: clear; sky still light; thin fingernail moon
scenes.action: Cranes settle on the riverbank as Gus and Call smoke and argue; later Call sees Lorena's shape greet Gus and lopes off to camp alone with the mare on her lead rope.

visualDetails: Gus rides a different horse from the one he left on; he calls it a 'piece of soap' too slow to chase Blue Duck.
Gus has white hair, easy to spot from a distance.
Both pigs are put in the wagon; the blue shoat jumps out and swims.
Po Campo's candy: hailstones dipped in molasses.
Lippy sits on the wagon seat.
Po Campo kills a crippled steer with one sharp axe blow and butchers it.
A flock of cranes lands on the river banks at dusk.
Night guard rides out; the Irishman sings to the herd.
Thin crescent moon in a still-light sky.

locations: Bill's Saloon - a two-storey clapboard saloon on the Trinity River bluffs, Fort Worth, Texas (whores upstairs, gamblers below)
Sally Skull's room with a small porch/balcony overlooking the wagon traffic of Fort Worth's streets
the Fort Worth jail
a saloon in Dallas, Texas (owned by a man named Ralph)
the trail north out of Dallas toward Kansas
mentioned: Montana, Austin, Georgia (Sally's past), Arkansas, Fort Smith, Kansas
events: Jake settles into Bill's Saloon in Fort Worth on a winning streak, paying Sally Skull ten dollars a day for her bed and the balcony view of cattle herds trailing north.
He snubs the Hat Creek hands when they visit, blaming them for Lorena's loss; Sally taunts him about letting an Indian take his woman.

Sally shoots a foreman with a derringer, is jailed, and dies alongside a deputy when they shoot each other struggling over his gun; Jake takes six hundred dollars from her hatbox and leaves for Dallas with her frightened girls.

In Dallas a soldier's news of an Arkansas sheriff and deputy searching Texas unnerves Jake, who then meets the three Suggs brothers and hears their 'regulator' scheme to tax herds at Kansas river crossings.
Fearing July Johnson, Jake rides north with the Suggs brothers and a black marksman called Frog Lip, planning to part ways at the first good Kansas saloon.
season: Not stated; roughly the same spring weeks as the herd's passage (the Hat Creek outfit passes Fort Worth during Jake's stay).
herdPosition: Hat Creek herd passed west of Fort Worth during Jake's first week there and is now well to the north (not stated in chapter).
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: the Suggs brothers (Dan, Roy, Ed) and Frog Lip. The text says the saloon owner is Bill Sloan (Sally 'ran the whoring establishment for Bill Sloan'); the Dallas bar owner is Ralph. Jake's pacing horse is not mentioned here. The soldier's report of an Arkansas deputy seeking his sheriff refers to Roscoe (dead by now). Jake notes Dallas is not far from Fort Smith. This chapter's timeline runs back to when the herd passed Fort Worth (overlaps ch59).

scenes.where: porch of Sally Skull's room at Bill's Saloon, Fort Worth
scenes.action: Jake props his feet on the porch rail watching wagons in the street while Sally joins him with a whiskey glass after setting her alarm clocks.
Sally uncorks the bedside whiskey, her green eyes dilated from powders, and asks why he let an Indian steal his whore.
Sally and the deputy fight over one gun and die together, half-naked, on the cell floor.
Roy Suggs spits tobacco on the floor ignoring the spittoon Ralph sets beside him while Dan pitches Jake the regulator scheme.
Frog Lip drops a deer at an impossible range as the party rides north.

mentionedCharacters: Roscoe Brown (the Arkansas deputy, unnamed by the soldier)
visualDetails: Bill's Saloon: two-storey clapboard building on the Trinity bluffs; from the top floor herds of cattle can often be seen moving north.
Five girls but three rooms; big alarm clocks outside the doors ring like fire bells after twenty minutes.

Sally Skull: tall and skinny, taller than most cowboys, short black hair, green eyes, bad teeth, bird-thin legs; oniony smell; drinks from waking; takes druggist's powders; buys dresses she wears once or twice; keeps a derringer under her pillow and a whiskey bottle by the bed.
Grimy, sweat-soaked sheets.
Six hundred dollars hidden in a hatbox.
The whores hire a buggy to go with Jake to Dallas.
Suggs brothers: scraggly beards, cold mean eyes; Dan oldest and talkative, heavy whiskey drinker; Ed and Roy sullen, watching the doors; Roy spits tobacco on the floor.
Frog Lip: tall black man, owns five guns of various calibres and constantly cleans them; superb marksman.
Jake buys a new rifle before leaving Dallas.

locations: empty high plains north of the Canadian River (Texas Panhandle / western Indian Territory)
a spot three days north of the Cimarron River where July's horse goes lame (likely southwestern Kansas / Neutral Strip area)
a dry camp on brown grass plains
a grove of low trees around a trickling spring with a ten-foot-wide pool
a running creek reached by following a wagon track
the Johns outfit's trail herd
Dodge City, Kansas
remembered: Fort Smith, the family cabin in Arkansas, the graves on the Canadian
events: Grieving the three dead buried on the Canadian, July rides north for days through empty country, eating mostly jackrabbit.
Three days north of the Cimarron a hidden cactus thorn lames his horse; he eventually shoots it and walks east with his rifle, weeping at the buzzards over it.
Out of water at a dry camp, he spends a moonlit night contemplating suicide with his pistol but decides he must first find Elmira and tell her about Joe.
Crows lead him to a spring in a grove of trees where he drinks, washes, and eats a badger he shoots.
He follows a wagon track to a creek, meets old trail boss Johns and buys a poor bay horse for forty dollars, then rides bareback four days into Dodge City.
season: Not stated; July left Gus about four days before the horse went lame, contemporaneous with the herd's Canadian crossing (spring). Johns's herd has been six weeks on the trail.
herdPosition: not stated in chapter
notes: July's route: north from the Canadian graves, across the Cimarron (named), then walking east, then a four-day bareback ride to Dodge City. Exact geography between the Cimarron and Dodge is not given. This is the 'July's walk to Dodge City' episode. July has never shot anyone in five years as a lawman. Uncle killed himself by drinking lye.

scenes.where: open prairie north of the Canadian
scenes.action: July rides alone under circling hawks and buzzards; a wolf lopes along a ridge.

scenes.where: tall prairie grass three days north of the Cimarron
scenes.action: July ties his horse down to dig a cactus thorn from its hoof, then later unsaddles and shoots the crippled animal.

scenes.weather: clear, moon climbing among bright stars
scenes.action: July sits on his blanket turning his pistol's cylinder, rifle barrel gleaming in moonlight, deciding not to kill himself yet. (memory of boyhood quilts in the Arkansas cabin)

scenes.where: grove of low trees with a small spring pool
scenes.timeOfDay: early grey morning through the day
scenes.weather: hot, shimmering sun on the prairie
scenes.action: Crows quarrel over a black snake curled on a rock by the pool; July drinks, bathes, dries his clothes on the grass and shoots a badger.

scenes.where: Johns's small trail herd, then the ride to Dodge
scenes.timeOfDay: day, departing under a rising moon
scenes.action: Cowboys gape at a lone man walking in from the west; July buys a sharp-spined little bay and rides off bareback toward Dodge.

visualDetails: Hawks and buzzards in a blue prairie sky; coyotes at night; jackrabbits.
Small spiky cactus hidden in tall grass.
A great cloud of buzzards over the dead horse, seen from a ridge.
July keeps his rifle and pistol but leaves his saddle with the dead horse.
Brown, wavy grass; shimmering plains.
Spring: a trickle forming a shallow pool about ten feet wide under low trees; black snake on a rock; crows in the trees.
A big badger.
Johns: old, white-mustached trail boss; his outfit six weeks on the trail.
July's new horse: the worst in the remuda, a little sharp-spined bay, ridden bareback.

locations: open, soggy plains of northern Kansas, south of the Republican River
the buffalo hunters' mule wagon loaded with hides
creeks where the wagon bogs
mentioned: the Republican River (not yet reached), 'the Fort' (their starting point - Bent's Fort on the Arkansas in Colorado, per ch53), Dodge City, Nebraska, Ogallala
events: Two weeks of rain, hail and lightning on the open plain leave Elmira, pregnant and wagon-sick, wondering whether fleeing July was worth it.
Luke repeatedly sneaks back from hunting to paw at her, knocks her off the wagon seat, and threatens to kill Zwey; she drives him off with Zwey's buffalo gun after the mules bolt.
That evening, as Elmira tells Zwey, an unseen rifle shot passes between them and knocks their roasting turkey into the ashes.
Luke returns, and one dawn tries to rape her with bloody hands; Zwey calmly smashes his head against the iron wagon wheel.
Elmira sews Luke's torn ear back on crookedly and nurses him through fever; Luke denies firing the turkey shot, leaving her afraid of an unknown watcher.
season: Not stated; wet stormy spring weather implied (two weeks of storms on the plain).
herdPosition: not stated in chapter
notes: Elmira's route: she travelled up the Arkansas by whiskey boat (ch36) and then by wagon to Bent's Fort (ch53); 'the Fort' in this chapter is Bent's Fort. From there Zwey and Luke drive her northeast across the plains; the chapter says they are driving across northern Kansas, not yet at the Republican River, bound for Ogallala. No nearer landmark is given. The unexplained turkey shot is left a mystery here. They have seen no one since leaving the Fort.

scenes.where: open plain in northern Kansas, in the hide wagon
scenes.weather: two weeks of rain, hail and lightning; soggy ground
scenes.action: Elmira bounces nauseous on the wagon seat and sleeps on wet blankets among stinking hides as the wagon bogs.
Luke shoves Elmira among the hides; the mules run away, Luke grabs the reins with his pants half down, and she levels Zwey's buffalo gun at him.
Zwey gnaws a turkey drumstick and cracks the bone for marrow; a shot from the darkness knocks the turkey off its stick and they dive under the wagon.
Luke, bloody from buffalo butchering, straddles Elmira; smiling Zwey drags him out and bashes his head against the wheel rim.
Elmira stitches Luke's dangling ear on lopsided while he yelps; later she drives alone and mistakes an antelope on a ridge for an Indian.

visualDetails: Mule-drawn wagon piled with smelly buffalo hides; rough ride.

Luke: small, feisty, mean crazy-looking eyes; sucks his fingers by the fire; after the beating his nose is bent sideways, one ear sewn on too low and misshapen, lips smashed, teeth broken, face swollen black.
Zwey: big, slow, strong as a mule, big face; sleeps like a rock; smiles while fighting.
Zwey's extra rifle is a heavy buffalo gun.
A wild turkey roasting on a stick, later eaten cold for breakfast.
Luke and Zwey cook slices of buffalo liver, bloody to the elbows; three fresh buffalo hides.
Elmira is visibly pregnant.
An antelope on a ridge mistaken for an Indian.

locations: northern Indian (Oklahoma) Territory, near the Kansas line
the south edge of Kansas, rolling prairie with humped rises to the north
the 'Blue Mounds' - low hills to the north that look blue at sunset and dawn (as named by Gus)
Gus and Lorena's tent camp about a mile from the herd
open plain where the grasshopper swarm strikes the herd
a low rise a mile or two north of Newt's stray bunch
mentioned: Santa Fe (Lippy's Apache wound), New Orleans (Gus's fortune-tellers), the Republican River, Arkansas (the fatal card game), Ogallala, Montana
characters: Bacon Rind (old Wichita with a milky eye)
five young Indians who guide Newt
ten or twelve young Indians given three beeves
events: Crossing the Territory the hands talk anxiously about Indians; Po Campo reads Gus's spit on the wagon boards and tells him he will marry no more.
Just before Kansas, five thin Wichitas led by an old one-eyed man Call knows as Bacon Rind ask for beef; Call gives them a lame steer and they exchange raised hands.
At dawn on the south edge of Kansas, Lorena, afraid Gus no longer wants her, offers herself free; Gus gently tells her to take her time.
A vast humming cloud of grasshoppers engulfs the plain at midday: Gus holds the terrified horses inside the tent with Lorena, while the herd stampedes and Newt is lost with about sixty cattle.
Young Indians lead the frightened Newt back to the herd; Soupy reports it is sixty miles to water to the north; Call refuses Newt's Dish-prompted request to check on Gus.
season: Not stated; still the wet spring/early summer of the drive (Jasper's arithmetic: about two months to cover a thousand miles).
herdPosition: Crossing from the Indian Territory into southern Kansas (Gus describes their camp as the south edge of Kansas); next river mentioned is the Republican; Indians say it is sixty miles to water due north.
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: the grasshopper swarm; Bacon Rind (a Wichita). The 'Blue Mounds' are named by Gus from hearsay; the text itself does not confirm the real-world identity. The implication is that the herd turns west toward water after the Indians' advice (the young Indians keep pointing west), though this is not spelled out. Jasper's horse throws him and he fears a broken collarbone. Po Campo tells Gus no more wives. The narrator lists the dead so far: Sean O'Brien, Bill Spettle, and July's three companions. Lippy claims an Apache wound from west of Santa Fe. Study-guide check: GradeSaver says the young Indians drive Newt's cattle 'westward towards the main herd' - consistent with the text (they point west; the herd lies over a low ridge).

scenes.action: Gus spits on the wagon boards among six chirping prairie-chicken chicks and Po Campo reads it; the skinny shoat rears up with forefeet on the wagon side.

scenes.where: drag of the herd near the Kansas line
scenes.action: Saddleless Wichitas on bony ponies cut out a split-hoofed steer; the old milky-eyed leader raises his hand to Call, who returns it.
Gus points out the Blue Mounds, humped rises to the north glowing an electric blue.

scenes.weather: dew-wet grass, warm sun; a brown cloud rising in the north

scenes.action: Grasshoppers coat the tent canvas and the lead ropes; Newt rides blind, hoppers in Mouse's mane, as the cattle run; Po Campo hides in the wagon under his serape.

scenes.weather: air clearing, thousands of hoppers still fluttering
scenes.action: Laughing hatless Indians handle Newt's pistol and hat, then drive his sixty strays over a low ridge to the herd and wagon.

Bacon Rind: skin and bones, one milky white eye; companions young, ponies thin, saddle blankets but no saddles, only one old carbine.

events: Camped north of Dallas, Jake hears the Suggses talk of killing, of July Johnson jailing two robbers with a rock-throwing girl, and of Dan's plan to steal a herd near Dodge and murder its crew.
At Doan's Store on the Red River, Jake flirts with a barefoot black-haired girl named Lou on a nester wagon; her seventy-odd-year-old husband clubs him with a ten-gauge shotgun.

When the old man raises the gun again Jake shoots him twice in the chest almost involuntarily; the girl oddly smiles at him, and with twenty or thirty nesters gathering he flees across the Red with the Suggses.
Half-drunk through the Territory, Jake secretly hopes to spot and rejoin the Hat Creek outfit while professing a grudge against Call and Gus.
In Kansas the gang terrorises a German sod-house family for four dollars, and Frog Lip stampedes their two milk cows through the sod roof.
season: Not stated; Dan predicts the farmer's crop 'along about July', implying late spring.
herdPosition: not stated in chapter (another, unnamed herd is crossing the Red near Doan's)
notes: This is the store where Jake shoots a man: Doan's Store on the Red River (named explicitly). Jake's second accidental killing (after Benny Johnson in Fort Smith). The two jailed robbers are those July and Janey captured earlier (Jim is one). 'Little Eddie' = Ed Suggs. Frog Lip says Blue Duck stole his horse. Jake's pacing horse is not mentioned. Settler family is German ('Dutchman'). The gang hopes to reach Dodge.

scenes.where: camp thirty miles north of Dallas
scenes.action: Little Eddie cooks while Frog Lip sits idle; the whiskey bottle circulates as Dan outlines stealing a herd and planting its cowboys.

scenes.weather: unspecified (Jake lounges in the store's shade)
scenes.action: Jake dusts his pants and strolls to the barefoot girl on the wagon seat, is slammed face-first into the dirt by a shotgun butt, then shoots the sandy-bearded old man, who slumps under the wagon.

Dan stands in his stirrups studying passing herds through old army spyglasses as the gang swings wide around them.

July watches cowboys load longhorns into boxcars, then drinks whiskey for hours waiting for Jennie, who tells him Ellie is surely chasing Dee in Ogallala.

After an awkward goodbye in which Jennie advises him to go home, July saddles Pete and rides out alone into the night.

scenes.where: outside stair landing above the main street

scenes.action: July lies vomiting over the edge clutching the rail, then sits watching the sun set behind a vast held herd as cowboys gallop into town through gilded dust, moonlight on the rail ties.

scenes.where: upstairs hallway, then the livery stable

locations: Kansas plains west of the grasshopper-stripped belt, with good grass, heading north toward the Arkansas River

While Ben Rainey rides Mouse to cut out a yearling, a small sharp-horned cow hooks Mouse behind the girth; Dish spares Newt by leading the dying horse off and shooting him.
After a night of hiding his tears on guard, Newt is invited to breakfast by Gus; Lorena smiles at him, and privately resolves to get Gus to marry her before Ogallala.
Call and Deets inspect the swift Arkansas by moonlight; Deets admits homesickness for the Rio Grande and reports crossing the track of Jake's pacing horse with four other horses to the east.
Call decides Jake is probably bound for Dodge, tells Deets to watch for the track, and sits up listening to the Irishman sing while a skunk passes his grazing mare.

scenes.where: edge of the herd at day's end
scenes.action: A small cow with twisty horns lifts Mouse's hindquarters off the ground; blood spurts from his belly, and Dish leads him a hundred yards off and shoots him, returning with the saddle.
Lorena, hair loose, holds a steaming coffee cup in both hands and smiles at Newt while the herd strings out north and tiny Po Campo walks far behind the wagon.
The hands pepper Newt with questions about Lorena as Dish bristles with jealousy.
Sitting their horses by the strong current, Call gazes upriver toward Colorado and Deets tells him of the pacing horse's track.

scenes.where: Call's camp a mile from the herd
scenes.action: A skunk noses and scratches between Call and the grazing mare, who ignores it, while the Irishman's singing drifts from the herd.

Gus's fire is made of buffalo chips.
Lorena's hair is loose around her shoulders; she sits on a pallet inside the tent flap.
The herd strung out north; wagon and remuda a mile behind; Po Campo a tiny dot walking behind the wagon.

Jake's pacing horse track with four other horses, crossed a few miles east.
The Hell Bitch staked out at night.

mentioned: Dodge City, Abilene, Denver, Nebraska, St. Louis, New Orleans, New York, the Mississippi, Arkansas (the dentist shooting), Mexico

events: Nearly at Dodge, Jake plans to slip away from the gang, but Dan Suggs spots his old boss Wilbarger driving about twenty-five horses south with two hands and resolves to steal them and kill him.
Frog Lip insolently orders Jake along; after a nap at a spring, the gang follows Wilbarger's trail northwest through dusk and swims the Arkansas by moonlight.
In a pitch-dark raid they kill Chick and a young wrangler in their blankets; Wilbarger escapes on horseback despite Dan claiming three hits, and Frog Lip is gut-shot.
At dawn Dan abandons Frog Lip, taking his guns; little Eddie shoots him in the head and rifles his pockets, and the gang drives the stolen horses north.

Coming on two settlers ploughing by a tent under a lone tree, Dan shoots both, takes a silver watch, hangs the corpses from the tree and burns them with coal oil; Jake, sickened, resolves to escape at the first chance.
season: Not stated; sunny weather.
herdPosition: not stated in chapter (Hat Creek herd not mentioned; ch70 puts it near the Arkansas, where Deets crossed the gang's tracks)
notes: The Suggs gang crosses the Arkansas River here, by moonlight, following Wilbarger northwest; they then head north toward Nebraska rather than to Abilene. Wilbarger is wounded (Dan claims three hits) and escapes; his fate is left open here. Frog Lip dies. Chick is identified as a hand seen when the Hat Creek men returned Wilbarger's horses from Mexico (Pedro Flores). Dan says Wilbarger has probably sold his lead herd in Dodge and has other herds bound for Denver. The settlers killed here are not named. Study-guide check: GradeSaver says Dan shoots Frog Lip; in the text Dan refuses and little Eddie shoots him in the head (TheBestNotes' vaguer 'they shoot' is consistent).

scenes.where: sunny Kansas prairie short of Dodge
scenes.action: Dan rides to a ridge and watches through spyglasses as three men drive a band of horses south; Frog Lip's blank stare dares Jake to follow.

scenes.where: spring with a few low trees
scenes.action: Dan naps with his hat over his face after threatening Jake, while Frog Lip sits cleaning his guns all afternoon.
The gang follows the horse tracks through the long dusk and swims the river in silence under the moon.

scenes.where: Wilbarger's dark camp north of the river
scenes.action: Rifle flashes erupt in the blackness and a horse gallops off; at dawn Chick lies nearly beheaded in his blankets and Frog Lip, sweat-bearded, lies bleeding from the groin before Eddie shoots him.

scenes.where: settlers' tent under a single small tree
scenes.action: Dan shoots two ploughmen, empties their trunk onto the grass, brews coffee, then hangs the bodies inches off the ground and sets their coal-oil-soaked clothes ablaze.

visualDetails: Wilbarger's horse band: about twenty-five horses, driven by three men.
Dan Suggs's war-surplus spyglasses.
Frog Lip rides behind Jake; carries a rifle and a big pistol in his belt; gut wound in the groin, pants soaked in blood.
Chick: weaselly, rabbit-toothed, shot through the neck; the other dead hand is a boy wrangler.
Settlers: two men in their forties with scraggly beards, ploughing with four mules; a tent under the only tree around.
A small trunk of clothes; a fine silver pocket watch taken by Dan.
Coal oil used to start a coffee fire and burn the hanged bodies; the dead men's feet a few inches above the ground; shoes still smouldering when the gang leaves.
Stolen mules added to the stolen horses.

locations: Hat Creek herd's crossing of the Arkansas River, Kansas, at a shallow, low-banked ford west of Dodge City (Gus doubts any herd has been trailed this far west of Dodge)
Open grassland a few miles north of the Arkansas where the herd grazes that afternoon

Wilbarger's grave on the bare Arkansas riverbank, marked with a cow-buffalo skull
events: Deets finds Wilbarger's big bay, blood-crusted, waiting on the north bank as the herd crosses the Arkansas; Dish's horse panics mid-river and Deets saves Dish, and the herd scatters into five or six bunches.
Deets backtracks the bay and reports Wilbarger shot three times by white horse thieves about ten miles off.
Call leaves Dish in charge of the herd and of Lorena, and rides east with Gus, Deets, Pea Eye and Newt.

Wilbarger names Dan Suggs and his brothers as his killers, bequeaths Gus his Milton and Virgil and the tent, gives his horse to Gus and asks his remaining horses be sold for his brother, then dies after dark.
They bury him on the bare bank with a cow-buffalo skull Deets fetches as a marker; Newt is given Wilbarger's rifle and Gus talks to him about the bones under the plains.
season: Midsummer - stated directly ('though it was midsummer, the skies clear').
herdPosition: Crossing the Arkansas River in Kansas, west of Dodge City; by midafternoon a few miles north of the Arkansas on ungrazed buffalo grass. Next major river: the Republican.
notes: Wilbarger's location: Deets returns 'along the river from the southeast' and the party rides east to reach him ~10 miles away, so he collapsed on the Arkansas downstream (east) of the crossing - between the herd and Dodge. Wilbarger was born on the Hudson, went to Yale, brother John Wilbarger at Fifty Broadway, New York City; he fought for the Union. FIRST APPEARANCE in this range of the buffalo-skull grave marker; Wilbarger's rifle becomes Newt's. The Hat Creek sign is recalled by Wilbarger (he praises Gus's sign). Study-guide discrepancy: GradeSaver says Dish's horse panicked because it smelled blood on Wilbarger's saddle - the text gives no reason, only that it took fright. Wilbarger's black companion who was shot is not named in this chapter (GradeSaver/Shmoop name him Frog Lip from ch71). The horse 'mean plug' Wilbarger gives Gus is presumably the bay.

scenes.action: Deets swims over ahead of Old Dog to catch a riderless bloody bay while Dish's horse thrashes in midstream and hundreds of cattle drift away downstream.

scenes.where: grassland a few miles north of the Arkansas
scenes.action: Deets comes loping along the river from the southeast on a sweat-streaked horse with news that Wilbarger is shot and dying.
Gus tells a shaking Lorena he must go and puts a dazzled Dish in charge of her, while Po Campo sings over supper and Newt swells with pride at being chosen.

scenes.action: Wilbarger lies on a blanket bleeding and joking with Gus while Newt stands weeping by the horses and Deets keeps watch on the riverbank.

locations: Hat Creek camp on the Kansas plains a few miles north of the Arkansas River

Night bed-ground farther north on the brown plain
characters: the Irishman (Allen O'Brien, singing, unnamed here)
events: Dish, now in charge, carries Lorena a plate of beef on horseback while Jasper and Soupy mock him; she takes it and shuts the tent.
Lippy lets slip to Dish that Gus once won Lorena on a cut of cards, paid her fifty dollars anyway, and paid Lippy ten to keep quiet.
Dish lies awake all night near her tent under the Kansas stars, then breakfasts her, strikes the tent and saddles her horse before taking the point.
At a small creek Po Campo gives Lorena sweet wild plums and tells her the cold water is snowmelt from far-off mountains.
Gus does not return; Lorena, fearing he is dead, lies sleepless in the tent while Dish keeps watch outside.
season: Midsummer (continues directly from ch72; 'months' since Lonesome Dove). Covers one night, the next day, and the second night.
herdPosition: North of the Arkansas River in western Kansas, easing north; crosses an unnamed small creek. Next major river: the Republican.

The Irishman singing to the cattle is Allen O'Brien (not named in this chapter). Lorena recalls Gus killing the Kiowas and buffalo hunters (her rescue). Study-guide discrepancies: Shmoop says Lorena and Po wash 'in a river' (text: a little creek) and that Dish finally realizes she will never love him (text: he refuses to give up while there is a chance). scenes.where: chuck wagon and Lorena's tent, camp north of the Arkansas
scenes.action: Dish rides the short way to the tent balancing a plate of beefsteak, and Lorena takes it and closes the flaps.

scenes.where: halfway between camp and the tent

scenes.action: Lippy blurts the story of Gus's fifty-dollar card cut, then Dish lies all night on his saddle listening to the Irishman sing to the cattle.
Dish arrives with breakfast as Lorena buttons her shirt, blushes, then rolls the tent and saddles her horse.

storyline: mixed (Hat Creek outfit; Jake & the Suggs)
events: They bury the buzzard-torn remains of Wilbarger's men and the Suggs's black rider; Deets reads Jake Spoon's sideways-riding track among the four thieves.

Late in the afternoon Call, Gus and Deets creep up the creek bed with the sun behind them; Deets wounds little Eddie and the rest are taken without a fight, Dan's boot derringer removed.

At a tree by the creek Deets fixes four nooses; Gus whips Dan's horse away and Eddie's bolts too, Roy follows, and Jake - after bidding his old partners farewell and giving Newt his pacing horse - spurs his own horse out from under himself.

season: Midsummer (day after ch72; same day as ch73's second day). Hangings at dusk, burial by moonlight.
herdPosition: Not with the herd; the herd is somewhere west, north of the Arkansas in Kansas, easing north under Dish.
notes: WHERE JAKE AND THE SUGGSES ARE HANGED: Kansas (Gus jokes they must be stopped 'before they wipe out Kansas'; Eddie says Dan claimed no man in Kansas could take him; Jake says he was only trying to get to Kansas). The creek is unnamed; it lies north of the Arkansas and roughly east of the herd (the party rides east in ch72 and afterwards drives the horses west to rejoin). No river is named for the hanging site - do not map it to the Arkansas itself. Collins's wagon was 'headed for Denver, I guess' per Call. Jake had about $800 won in Fort Worth poker. FIRST APPEARANCE: Jake's pacing horse as Newt's mount (Newt's other horse is turned into the herd, still saddled). Dan Suggs left hanging. Study-guide discrepancies: Shmoop says Eddie was shot reaching for his rifle (text: his pistol) and implies Newt's horse had just died (Mouse died earlier; here Newt simply switches horses); GradeSaver names the black rider Frog Lip - the text here calls him only the bad black man. Burials: Jake, Roy, Eddie and Collins; Dan left up.

Deets finds no water ahead; Call rides the Hell Bitch about 60 miles to Salt Creek's pools and straight back, reporting water some 80 miles off, and decides to push on.
Driving through the night and day, the herd is hit by a hot sandstorm at a blood-red sunset; cattle scatter until it dies after three hours.
In brutal heat the cattle go thirst-blind and the Irishman grows delirious; the sleepless Call dozes in the saddle and wakes to find Deets leading his mare.

events: After two days' rest on Salt Creek, Indians on foot steal twelve horses at night while the men sing; Call, Gus and Deets ride after them, leaving orders to graze the herd upriver toward the Powder.
After more than a hundred miles of rattlesnake badlands they find a tiny starving band eating one of the horses; Call fires in the air to scatter them.
Deets picks up a blind toddler left sprawled in the horse's entrails; a teenage brave charges with an old lance and drives it into Deets's chest; Call and Gus shoot the boy, and Deets dies.
Leaving the band three poor horses, they carry Deets's body back and catch the herd before dawn; Newt wakes to see the body and weeps unnoticed.

notes: WHERE DEETS DIES: in a draw in barren, salt-streaked country more than a hundred miles southwest of the Salt Creek camp, i.e. Wyoming (the chapter's surrounding text says they are on the Wyoming plain; the territory is not named at the death site). Gus mentions the Wind River as the direction the thieves were heading; the band's tribe is only Gus's guess (Ute). Deets is BURIED on a rise north of where Salt Creek joins the Powder. Board paraphrase: his name, thirty years' service with Call, 21 fights with Comanche and Kiowa, cheerful in all weathers, never shirked, splendid behaviour (with Call's misspellings such as 'CHERFUL'). Callback to Gus's Hat Creek sign that troubled Deets over his first name.
