Holed up in a creek bed, they lose both horses to a knife-wielding Indian, Gus kills several attackers, and they dig a cave under a steep bank where Gus forces the deep arrow through his leg and faints.
A cloudburst floods the creek; with Gus feverish, he sends Pea to swim downstream at night and fetch Call, and Pea loses his clothes, rifle and food in the current.
Pea walks naked and barefoot south for about three days, feeling Deets beside him, until Dish spots him north of the herd; Call puts Dish in charge and rides north alone to find Gus.
season: Late summer turning to autumn: the men fear winter, a cloud bank brings talk of snow, and Pea is caught in a wet snow squall one night followed by a blazing hot day two days later. No month named.
herdPosition: At the start the herd is still south of the Yellowstone (Gus reckons over a hundred miles from the fight site and not yet at the river). By the end the herd crossed the Yellowstone the day before Pea is found, and Call orders it moved on north. Miles City is the nearest town.
notes: The attackers are never identified in this chapter (Gus jokes they did not introduce themselves); ch95 has Hugh Auld name them Blood Indians. The fight is NOT on the Yellowstone itself but on a creek three-plus days north of it and short of the Milk; in ch96 Call calls it the Musselshell River (real-world the Musselshell lies west of Miles City and flows north to the Missouri, so the novel's geography is loose). GradeSaver says about 40 warriors; text says at least twenty. TheBestNotes calls the attackers Utes, which the text never does. Gus's arrows are in his LEFT leg. Gus's kill count: three from the bank, the Indian boy and a second man in the brush, then one on the far bank in the flood (Hugh later hears seven). Deets is placed as buried on the Powder River. Pea recalls the grizzly that fought the Texas bull. The crew boasts of being the first to bring a Texas herd across the Yellowstone. Gus carries his own big Henry rifle here (not to be confused with Call's Henry, which Call gives Newt in ch100).

scenes.where: Hat Creek camp on the plain
scenes.weather: breezy, dark cloud bank in the northwest, talk of snow
scenes.action: Gus stuffs extra ammunition in his saddlebags and lopes off with Pea while the melancholy crew watches; they pass Po Campo hunting wild onions a mile out.

scenes.where: Yellowstone River and the prairie beyond
scenes.weather: clear blue sky after the clouds blew away
scenes.action: Fifty or sixty buffalo scatter from the river; Gus drinks cold water from his hands mid-crossing, then races alongside the running herd just for the joy of it.

scenes.where: Grassy rise and open prairie north of the Yellowstone
scenes.weather: crisp early, then sunny and warm
scenes.action: Gus comes racing back down a slope with twenty-odd mounted Indians firing guns and arrows behind him; the pair gallop several miles to a brushy creek.

scenes.where: Creek bend with a sheer ten-foot bank; shallow cave dug beneath it
scenes.timeOfDay: dusk into night, then a stormy dawn
scenes.weather: still at dusk; later thunder, lightning and a long hard cold rain that floods the creek
scenes.action: Arrows rain over the bank, Pea cuts the arrowhead free as Gus faints, war cries echo and Gus answers with a Comanche yell; the brown flood rises to within yards of the cave.

scenes.where: Open plains south toward the Yellowstone; the herd's camp
scenes.timeOfDay: night swim; days of walking; found two hours after sunup
scenes.weather: cloudy dark night, a wet snow squall, then a blazing hot day
scenes.action: Naked, sunburned and with swollen bleeding feet, Pea sits in the grass talking to the unseen Deets until Dish and Call find him and wrap him in Call's slicker.

mentionedCharacters: Deets (dead, buried on the Powder; Pea believes his ghost guides him)
Jake Spoon (described the Milk and Marais)
Barlow (old acquaintance hooked by a buffalo)
the Irishman (Allen O'Brien, whose singing Pea listens for)
the old blind Comanche who taught Gus a war cry
visualDetails: Jasper has made himself crude floats from empty lard buckets for fear of deep rivers.
Pea sharpens his knife before any trip; he ties his bedroll on and carries a rifle.
Fifty or sixty buffalo at the Yellowstone; smaller bunches of twenty or thirty farther north; the pair eat the liver of a crippled buffalo calf while buzzards and prairie wolves wait.
The prairie north of the river is brown in the distance with grass waving in the breeze.
The Indians' horses are poorer than the Hat Creek horses; attackers use both guns and arrows and shelter behind their horses out of range.
Gus fires his big Henry rifle from under his propped-up saddle and drops five or six Indian horses.
Both scouts' horses are found with throats cut, bright blood on green weeds.
Gus takes an old cap-and-ball pistol and an old Sharps carbine from the dead Indian boy; the carbine stock serves as a shovel.
Gus plasters his wound with a cannonball-sized handful of creek mud.
Pea's shoulder is shot clean through above the shoulder blade; he ends up stark naked, sunburned, feet swollen and cut, blood on his chest.
Call is shoeing the mare (the Hell Bitch), who must be snubbed to allow it; he lends Pea his slicker and Dish buttons it for him.
Po Campo spoon-feeds Pea coffee against the wagon.

locations: Cave under the creek bank where Gus was besieged (the Musselshell per Call in ch96), north of the Yellowstone, Montana Territory
Open plain southeast of the creek, on the way to Miles City (about forty miles from where Hugh finds Gus)
Slope north of the Yellowstone overlooking Miles City four or five miles to the east
Miles City, Montana Territory: street in front of a saloon
characters: men of Miles City outside the saloon
events: Feverish and delirious, Gus watches the black water all night for Indians floating down on logs, drifting in thought to Clara.

At sunny dawn, with his leg yellow and black-streaked from blood poisoning, he builds a crutch from the Indian carbine and his cut stirrups and hobbles southeast toward Miles City, finding the Indians gone after buffalo.
He collapses in the night and wakes at noon to find old trapper Hugh Auld squatting over him with a bowie knife, considering taking off the rotten leg.
Hugh names the attackers as Blood Indians, lends Gus his spotted horse Custer, and ties him into the saddle.
Gus reaches Miles City at dark, fires his pistol to summon help, and is thrown into the street by the skittish horse just as he is untied and passes out.
season: Autumn: Gus notes winter is coming and the Indians need buffalo before it; the dawn is sunny and hot. Month not stated.
herdPosition: Not stated in chapter; Gus guesses the herd may have moved north faster than he reckoned but expects Call to be days away. Miles City lies on the Yellowstone, southeast of the fight.
notes: FIRST APPEARANCE: Hugh Auld (Old Hugh) and his spotted horse Custer. Hugh identifies the war party as Blood Indians and says he gets along with Bloods and Blackfeet from the beaver-trading days; TheBestNotes wrongly frames it as 'Blood, not Utes' (Utes never appear). TheBestNotes has Hugh and Gus riding into town together; in the text Hugh stays behind and says he will follow on foot. Hugh claims seven dead Indians; Gus says five. Miles City is reached in about five hours; Gus sees the town four or five miles east from a slope north of the Yellowstone, so the town is on the river's north side in the novel's geography. Hugh says Miles City has two doctors, both drunkards. Gus tells Hugh he comes from Lonesome Dove on the Rio Grande. Gus introduces himself as a Captain in the Texas Rangers.

scenes.where: Cave under the flooded creek bank
scenes.action: Shaking with fever, Gus sits with pistol cocked watching the dark water, seeing Clara's face in delirium.

scenes.where: Receding creek, a game trail up the bank, then open plain
scenes.weather: sunny and hot; Gus sweats yet feels chilled
scenes.action: Gus lashes stirrups to the Indian carbine as a crutch and drags himself southeast across the empty plain, crossing fresh tracks of a big buffalo herd, resting standing up.
(dream of Lorena and a red sun first) Gus wakes to a tiny, bent old man in patched buckskins spitting tobacco and holding a bowie knife, a spotted horse grazing nearby.

scenes.where: Slope north of the Yellowstone, then Miles City street
scenes.action: Tied to the saddle, Gus fires three shots in front of a saloon; men untie him, the spotted horse bucks him into the street and bolts back out of town.

mentionedCharacters: Lorena Wood (in a fever dream of the tent in Kansas)
visualDetails: Gus's leg turns yellow with black streaks, and by noon the next day simply black.
Crutch: the Indian boy's carbine with a stirrup lashed over each end, one end padded with saddle leather.
Gus carries one pistol in his belt, one holstered, his rifle, and a pocketful of jerky.
Hugh Auld: very old, scarcely five feet tall, back permanently bent from a deadfall accident, tobacco-stained beard, patched buckskins, bowie knife; says he is probably not yet eighty.
Hugh's horse Custer is spotted, bucks if kicked, bites strangers, and is named for the general Hugh once scouted for.
Hugh ties a rawhide loop around Gus's waist fastened to the cantle.
Gus's delirium: a red world, lying on a swollen red sun sinking into the plain.

locations: Small hot upstairs room in Miles City, Montana Territory, with a window onto the prairie, across the street from a saloon with a piano
Miles City street below the window
Remembered/planned: Clara's orchard, a little grove of live oaks on the south Guadalupe River, Texas
Mentioned: the Musselshell River (where Gus holed up), Nebraska (Clara's), San Antonio (Gus's bank), Tennessee (Gus's youth)
characters: Dora (pockmarked consumptive pianist, seen in the street)
events: Gus wakes to find his left leg amputated by the drunken Dr. Mobley and refuses at gunpoint to let him take the blackened right leg.
He drinks through the afternoon, tosses a gold piece to Dora, the saloon pianist, and eats venison he cannot keep down.
Call arrives at night, having found the fight site and Pea's gear, and fails to talk Gus into the second amputation.
Gus asks to be buried in Clara's orchard on the Guadalupe in Texas, leaves his half of the herd to Lorena, tells Call he told Newt the truth, and asks for the Hat Creek sign over his grave.
Gus writes notes to Clara and Lorena, asks that Pea get his saddle, and dies at nightfall while Call dozes.
season: Autumn (cool night). Gus proposes the body wait the winter and travel in spring. About two days after Call left the herd.
herdPosition: Gus believes the herd should be north of the Yellowstone by now; Call says they found Pea Eye only the day before.
notes: Burial site named explicitly: a little grove of live oaks on the south Guadalupe, called Clara's orchard because Gus and Clara picnicked there; Gus reminds Call they stopped there briefly (the earlier chapter on the way toward Austin). Call identifies the siege creek as the Musselshell River, learned from the old trapper. Call rode the Hell Bitch day and night, recovered Pea Eye's rifle, boots and shirt and Gus's saddle before reaching Miles City. Gus refuses revenge on the Indians. FIRST APPEARANCE: Dr. Mobley, Dora. The Hat Creek sign is confirmed to be riding in the wagon and Gus asks it be placed over his grave. Gus's jug is alluded to (the springhouse). Shmoop is accurate here; GradeSaver omits the sign request.

scenes.action: Out of a red fever-dream, Gus wakes one-legged beside a snoring fat doctor in a dandruffy black frock coat and demands the whiskey bottle.

scenes.where: Same room and the street below
scenes.action: Gus levels his pistol to send the stooping giant Jim away, then flips a twenty-dollar gold piece out the window to the pockmarked girl in black, who goes back in and plays again.

scenes.where: Same room, lantern on the bureau
scenes.action: Call looks at the black leg and Gus cocks his pistol on him; they talk of burial in Texas, Lorena, Newt and the sign.
Gus gazes out at Montana, scrawls two notes, drifts into a silvery Tennessee-morning mist; later the doctor's lamp shows blood dripping from the sheet.

mentionedCharacters: Bolivar, Lippy, Pedro Flores, Gus's two wives and three sisters (in delirium)
visualDetails: Dr. Mobley: small, fat, red-streaked cheeks, black frock coat sprinkled with dandruff, disreputable old bowler hat on the bureau.
Gus's left leg is gone; the thick stump bandage is leaking blood; the remaining leg is black.
Jim is so tall he must stoop in the doorway and bumps his head leaving.
Dora: skinny, pockmarked, in a black dress; she is said to have studied music in Philadelphia.
Bartender: timid, with a walrus mustache as good as Dish Boggett's; brings venison.
Gus sails a twenty-dollar gold piece into the street.
Gus vomits into a brass spittoon.
Call carries a lantern; one note is left on the bed with a little blood on it, which Call wipes on his pants leg.

locations: Miles City, Montana Territory: Gill's livery stable, the carpenter's, the hardware store, Dr. Mobley's harness shed, the dry goods store
Salt lick about six miles north of Miles City, reached by game trails
A little stream on the plain where Call sits for hours on the ride back
The herd spread over the great plain north of the Yellowstone (Hugh plans to catch up north of the Musselshell)
events: Dr. Mobley offers to pack Gus's body in charcoal and salt and store it in his harness shed until spring; Call has a sturdy coffin made and hauls salt from a lick six miles north.
Gus, his amputated leg, charcoal and salt are sealed in the coffin, which is set on two barrels in the shed.
Call buys winter coats and building supplies, hires Old Hugh to drive them north in a rented wagon, and rides back slowly, grieving and resentful.
At the herd, Dish and Needle report a watching band of Indians with women and children (Call guesses Crow); Call tells the men Gus is dead.
Newt weeps on the drag; around the fire the men puzzle over the leg and the Texas burial, and Dish resolves to leave for Lorena when the drive ends.
season: Autumn, just before winter: a cool wintry wind follows a hot day; Call says Gus will be above ground until next summer.
herdPosition: North of the Yellowstone, grazing across the plain; Hugh expects to catch up north of the Musselshell. Miles City is the nearest town behind them.
notes: The carpenter's name, Joe Veitenheimer, is given by Gill as a recommendation; Call then finds 'the carpenter' (presumably him). Gus died day before yesterday by the time Call reaches the herd. The Indians watching the herd are only guessed to be Crow by Call. Call counts Jake dead in Kansas and Deets in Wyoming. The blue pigs are present (under the wagon) - they will be eaten at Christmas in ch100. The Texas-burial wager: Lippy bets Call won't do it, Dish takes the bet. Soupy recalls hearing Gus was from Tennessee.

scenes.action: Call lies sleepless on straw; at sunup the limping, milky-eyed Gill forks hay and the mare snakes out her neck to bite him.

scenes.where: Salt lick six miles north of town
scenes.action: Antelope scatter from the lick as Call sweats, scooping salt into a borrowed wagon amid buffalo and elk tracks.

scenes.where: Undertaker's and Dr. Mobley's harness shed
scenes.action: Men pack charcoal and salt around Gus, his face covered with a new bandana, nail the coffin shut and set it on two barrels.

scenes.where: In front of the dry goods store, then a little stream on the plain
scenes.weather: cloudy, cool wintry wind after a hot day
scenes.action: Call hires Old Hugh to drive the supply wagon, then sits alone by a stream for hours before riding on through the night.

scenes.where: Herd grazing over three miles of plain; the wagon and campfire
scenes.action: Call tells the news tersely and rides off alone; Newt cries hidden in the drag dust; at night Po jingles his tambourine and the Irishman whistles sadly.

visualDetails: Old man Gill: rheumatic limp, rusty beard, one milky eye; later sits drinking from a jug in a wheelbarrow, pitchfork across his lap, hooking one finger through the jug loop like Gus.
The undertaker is tall and trembles constantly from a nervous disease.
Call buys a fine bandana to cover Gus's face; the amputated leg is wrapped in burlap soaked in formaldehyde.
Coffin filled to the top with salt and nailed shut, set on two empty barrels in the harness shed.
Old Hugh sits in front of the dry goods store; he drives a mule wagon of coats, overshoes, gloves and building supplies.
The herd spreads three miles across the plain; Lippy drives the wagon; Pea Eye rides in the back, still barefoot.
Both pigs sleep under the wagon, grunting and snoring.
Po Campo's tambourine; the Irishman whistling.

locations: Missouri River crossing near Fort Benton, Montana Territory (tiny Army outpost)
Marais River (crossed; Old Dog lost the next day)
Milk River, the last river before Canada, with snow-covered Rockies visible to the west
Ranch headquarters: a timbered creek off the Milk River, a day's drive east of where they first struck it; range between the Milk and the Missouri
Box canyon about fifteen miles from headquarters where wild horses are caught
Fort Benton and Fort Buford (beef delivery trips); Missouri River ice at Fort Benton
Mentioned: Miles City bank, Nebraska, the Yellowstone, south of the Brazos
events: Old Hugh rejoins with the supply wagon; the outfit crosses the icy Missouri near Fort Benton, where Major Court buys two hundred head and Jasper is nearly drowned when a beaver spooks his horse.
The day after crossing the Marais, two grizzlies are found eating Old Dog, setting off a stampede; a few days later the herd reaches the Milk River.

Call picks a timbered creek for headquarters, ends the drive, and a three-day blizzard hits while the men build a log house, with Po Campo making the fireplace and chimney; Call lives in Wilbarger's tent.
The men capture eighteen wild horses in a box canyon, and Dish, riding Sugar with a spare buckskin, leaves for Nebraska to court Lorena.
Call wins an Army contract for three hundred beeves by Christmas; Newt proves a gifted bronc rider and spends a month breaking horses at Fort Benton, once crashing through the Missouri ice.
season: Autumn into winter: several light snows before the Missouri, a crisp fall day at the Milk, then blizzards; Call's contract is for delivery by Christmas; Newt's month at Fort Benton falls later in the winter.
herdPosition: Crosses the Missouri near Fort Benton, then the Marais, then reaches the Milk River; driven a day east along the Milk to the headquarters creek. The drive is over; the range lies between the Milk and the Missouri.
notes: Ranch site: a creek with sheltering timber off the Milk River, a day east of where they struck it; Call will file on the land in spring. Old Hugh says north of the Milk is Canada. Old Dog (the lead steer) dies here, eaten by two grizzlies. Dish leaves on Sugar. Call keeps Gus's letters rather than risk them with Dish. Fort Buford is also named as a beef customer. The Blackfoot trade and the Blood Indians seen at Fort Benton: Call suspects some were Gus's killers. GradeSaver says 'an outpost near Fort Benton'; the text calls the outpost Fort Benton itself. The novel's own text misprints the name as 'Old High Auld' in the chapter's opening line. The pigs are not mentioned this chapter.

scenes.where: North bank of the Missouri near Fort Benton
scenes.action: The men build a huge bonfire; blue-lipped Jasper sits wrapped in blankets after Ben Rainey pulls him from the icy river.

scenes.where: Trail behind the herd past the Marais
scenes.action: Riding back for the missing lead steer, the drag riders find two grizzlies feeding on Old Dog; the horses bolt and the whole herd and remuda stampede.

scenes.timeOfDay: day and night over three days
scenes.weather: howling blizzard, no visibility, then a hard crust and deeper cold
scenes.action: The crew huddles between two big fires; Dish's mustache freezes; Po Campo in his serape urges them to shoot a bear.

scenes.weather: light snowfall overnight, plains white for miles
scenes.action: Call writes Dish's wage order on a tablet resting on a frying pan; Dish rides off on Sugar leading a little buckskin until he is a black speck on the snow.

scenes.where: Sapling corral at headquarters; later Fort Benton and the Missouri ice
scenes.weather: cold but often fine and sunny
scenes.action: Newt murmurs to a hammer-headed bay while Call watches silently from the mare; later a runaway sorrel carries him onto the river ice and breaks through in shallow water.

mentionedCharacters: Augustus McCrae (dead; appears in Call's dreams)
visualDetails: Major Court: lanky; Fort Benton is a tiny, poorly provisioned outpost.
The great line of the Rockies is visible to the west; the mountain slopes are snow-covered at the Milk.
Most men wear their new coats at the Milk on a crisp fall day.
The Texas bull is now one-eyed and one-horned with an unevenly sewn wound, and leads the herd; he attacks from his blind side.
Sizable rough log cabin with Po Campo's mud-brick fireplace and chimney; later corrals, a smokehouse and a barn begun.
Call sleeps in Wilbarger's old tent on the creek with a small fire in front.
Po Campo wears a serape and an old scarf; Newt ties a flannel shirt over his ears.
The wild horses are smallish and fat; Bert Borum ropes eighteen.
Dish rides Sugar and leads a little buckskin; he is loaded with provisions and a rifle.
A strong black mustang throws Ben Rainey into a tree and breaks his arm; Newt rides it to a standstill.
Blackfoot chief the soldiers call Saw for his sharp features; Blood Indians also present at the fort.
Fort Benton is full of Indians when beef is delivered; buffalo and elk meat pile up at the ranch.

locations: Clara Allen's horse ranch on the Platte River, Nebraska (near Ogallala per earlier chapters; not named here): kitchen, upstairs sickroom, tool shed, horse lots, upper porch
Mentioned: the Platte River (Dish's route), Wyoming, Texas, Montana
events: In the first week of the new year July blurts a marriage proposal as he brings frozen potatoes into the kitchen; Clara answers only by asking him to taste her cake batter.
Baby Martin falls dangerously ill; Clara keeps a lone vigil, briefly clings to July, and next morning in the cold scolds him for not sitting with her and tells him to ask again in a year.
Dish Boggett arrives through a January blizzard along the Platte with news of Gus's death; Clara hires him, and July grows jealous of his skill.
Lorena sinks into silent grief, close only to Betsey; Clara tells her Gus loved them both but could never be kept home.
Dish courts Lorena hopelessly all winter, yet stays in spring to help with the colts.
season: Winter: first week of the new year (January) for the proposal; Dish arrives in a January blizzard; the chapter runs through the winter into spring (colts coming).
herdPosition: n/a - chapter set at Clara's ranch in Nebraska
notes: The ranch is not named in this chapter; earlier chapters place it near Ogallala on the Platte. Martin is July's son by Elmira. Clara's 'ask me in a year' is the only answer to the proposal. GradeSaver says Dish 'decides to stay the winter' - in fact Clara offers him a job; at chapter's end he stays past spring for the colts. Clara reveals Gus proposed to her thirty-odd times and looked relieved when she chose Bob. Lorena calls herself a whore aloud for the first time. The sorrel stallion is Clara's favourite (not to be confused with the little sorrel she gave Newt).

scenes.action: July sets down a sack of frozen potatoes and asks Clara to marry him; she holds out a batter-covered finger for him to taste.
Clara rocks the rasping, feverish baby's cradle, then abruptly lays her head on July's chest in tears.

scenes.weather: sunny but very cold; breath clouds
scenes.action: July is taking a cracked wagon wheel off when Clara storms over, refuses his offered coat, lays into him, then rubs her favourite stallion's neck.

scenes.where: Big kitchen table at night; Clara's icy upper porch
scenes.action: Dish plays cards and charades with Clara and the girls while Lorena and July sit silent against the wall; later Clara sits alone on the porch in Bob's huge coat, a cold tear on her cheek.
Clara hugs the uncombed, grief-struck Lorena and later explains why neither woman could have kept Gus home.

mentionedCharacters: Elmira (July's late wife, implied as Martin's mother)
visualDetails: Martin is a crawling baby who laughs and grabs spoons.

Clara in winter wears her late husband's oversized coat and overshoes, no gloves, large bony hands, and caps, favourite being an old Army cap Cholo found on the plains, sometimes with a wool scarf tied over it; her hair spills over the collar.
Clara has gray eyes.
Clara's favourite horse is a sorrel stallion that whinnies from the lots.
Upper porch crusted with ice; stars dimmed by cold.
Dish arrives with two exhausted horses after following the Platte in a January blizzard.
Lorena, still beautiful but grave, uncombed; Betsey reads stories to her since Lorena can barely read.

locations: Hat Creek ranch headquarters on a creek off the Milk River, Montana Territory: log house, corrals, Wilbarger's tent
Nearby Indian camps (Blackfeet among them) visited with Old Hugh
Horsethieves' camp just across the border in Canada, a day north of the line (caught on the third day)
Fort Benton (Newt's test cattle sale; source of new hands and horses)
Banks of the Milk River where cattle bog, with Canada lying behind Newt to the north
Mentioned: Miles City (bank for Lorena's share; source of two new cowboys), Missouri (Big Tom's forge), Kentucky, Oregon, Mississippi (Call's father's death), Nebraska
events: Call resents banking half of every sale for Lorena, lives in Wilbarger's tent all winter, and at Christmas the men kill Gus's pigs; Jasper learns to cook under Po Campo.

In early spring fifteen horses are stolen; Call's party tracks them into Canada, shoots the drunken old preacher who wounds Needle with a hatchet, spares his son Tom, then hangs him ten days later for stealing wallets and Bert's saddle.
Call gives Newt growing responsibility; Soupy objects, trips Newt and beats him in a fight, then leaves with Bert for Texas while new hands drift in.
After a ten-day roundup and a week of branding in May, Call spends afternoons watching Newt break horses but cannot tell him he is his son.
At the end of May Call names Newt range boss, gives him the Hell Bitch, his Henry rifle and his father's gold watch, and rides away south with Greasy, Jerry and the Hat Creek sign.
season: Winter through spring: pigs killed at Christmas; horse theft in early spring with thin snow; branding with spring grass through thin May snows; Call leaves toward the end of May, the body now about six months dead.
herdPosition: Ranch established; cattle spread over the range between the Milk and the Missouri; several hundred calves born since Texas are branded.
notes: FATE OF THE BLUE PIGS: killed and eaten at Christmas. The Hell Bitch passes to Newt, along with Call's Henry rifle and his father's gold watch. FIRST APPEARANCE by name: Jerry the dun (Greasy the mule is older). Call sets out WITHOUT the body; it is still in Mobley's shed at Miles City (ch101). Call tells Newt he'll be gone about a year and to bank Lorena's half in Miles City. Pea mentions Call hanged Jake. GradeSaver says Call makes Newt boss before the Soupy fight; broadly right. TheBestNotes claims Call sends Newt to Fort Benton to break horses again - text says he sends Newt to sell cattle. Shmoop says Tom tried to steal a horse; he also took four wallets and Bert's saddle. Newt says bitterly he is kin to nobody.

scenes.where: Horsethieves' camp on the prairie in Canada
scenes.action: Call walks in with pistol drawn on a drunk graybeard reading a Bible and a huge sweaty boy cooking venison; the old man swings a hatchet at Needle and Call shoots him.
Call shoots Big Tom off a stolen horse, clubs him with the Henry barrel, and hangs him as the men watch in silence.

scenes.where: Around the supper fire at headquarters
scenes.action: Soupy trips Newt carrying his plate; Newt flies at him and is pounded bloody while Call watches impassively.
For two weeks Call sits for hours silently watching Newt gentle the new horses.

scenes.where: Muddy banks of the Milk River
scenes.action: Mud-caked from lifting bogged yearlings, Newt saddles the Hell Bitch with his own saddle as Call, choking on words, gives him the Henry and a thin gold watch and rides off to a speck on the plain.

visualDetails: Lippy tries all winter to build a fiddle from a shoebox, producing screeching.
Old preacher: shaky, dirty gray beard, single-shot buffalo gun, a jug by his saddle, muttering over a Bible.
Big Tom: big as an ox, about Newt's age, large always-sweaty face, cap-and-ball pistol; a blacksmith who shoes all the horses.
No decent hanging tree for miles on the plain.
Newt at seventeen has filled out physically; Pea says he walks just like Call.
Greasy is the big mule that came from Texas; Jerry is a rangy dun, Call's second-favourite mount.
Gus's old sign is tied to the pack mule.
Newt had been riding the little sorrel Clara gave him.
Call's Henry fits Newt's scabbard imperfectly, replacing Newt's Winchester.
Call's father's watch: old pocket watch with a thin gold case.
The one-eyed Texas bull bellows and paws with a few cows a hundred yards off.

locations: Miles City, Montana Territory: Dr. Mobley's harness shed, the carpenter's
Plains south of Miles City, riding alongside about a hundred Crow Indians
Wyoming: eleven empty days; gullies near the Powder River
Approach to Nebraska; the Platte River, full of ducks and geese
Clara Allen's horse ranch in Nebraska (near Ogallala per earlier chapters): house, lots, back porch, the buggy by the yard, the shack by the lots
characters: old Crow chief and his band
events: In Miles City Call finds an animal broke into the shed, splintered the coffin and carried off Gus's amputated leg; he has the coffin reinforced and buys an old buggy, tearing off its ragged hood.
He travels south with a friendly Crow band, through empty Wyoming and past the Powder, and faces down five drunk young Indians near Nebraska.
At Clara's ranch Clara berates him for hauling the body and urges burial there; he hands over Gus's two notes, and Clara sobs against the mule.
Lorena stands beside the coffin all night clutching her unread note; Clara reads hers privately, in which Gus asks her to look after Lorena.
Lorena faints next morning; Call hitches up and leaves while Clara strides beside his horse denouncing him for abandoning his unnamed son.
season: Late spring into early summer, inferred: Call left the Milk at the end of May; the Miles City departure is on an unseasonably cold morning; the Platte teems with ducks and geese. No month named.
herdPosition: n/a - Call is travelling south with the body; the herd remains on the Milk River ranch.
notes: Route south: Miles City, riding with Crow, Wyoming (eleven days without a soul), gullies near the Powder River, then Nebraska along the Platte. The amputated leg is lost to an animal. Clara refers to Newt as Call's son outright and vows to write Newt so he gets Call's name. Call says he values the horse more than the name. Clara says she kept Gus in memory for sixteen years. July recalls Gus killing the Kiowa at a campfire. Clara's ranch is unnamed here (Ogallala area per ch76-77). Gus's note to Clara is quoted in the novel; here only paraphrased: he asks her to look after Lorie and wishes her luck with the horses. Shmoop says Call 'bundles Gus up' in Miles City - he actually keeps the reinforced coffin until the Pecos (ch102).

scenes.where: Dr. Mobley's shed, Miles City; then the road out
scenes.weather: unseasonably cold, pale sun through frigid clouds
scenes.action: Call leaves town with a heavy plank-reinforced, canvas-covered coffin lashed to the seat of a hoodless buggy drawn by Greasy.
A dried-up little chief hungry for tobacco and talk rides beside Call among a hundred Crow, all curious about the man in the box.
Bareheaded Clara in overshoes, planting shrubs, turns on Call; after taking the notes she presses her face to the mule's neck and weeps.

scenes.where: By the buggy in the yard; Clara's upper porch
scenes.action: Lorena stands like a statue by the coffin all night holding her letter; Clara sits an hour on her porch twisting her hands.
Lorena crumples and is carried upstairs; Call trots the dun and the mule away, the squeaking buggy bouncing, as Clara strides alongside raging.

mentionedCharacters: Kiowa raiders July saw Gus kill (memory)
visualDetails: The coffin is splintered by a wolverine or cougar (doctor's guess), then reinforced with strong planks and covered in canvas.
Old sturdy buggy, hood torn off; Greasy (a brown mule, normally skittish, used to the wagon) pulls it; Call rides the dun, Jerry.
Greasy loses flesh from the pace.
Five drunk Indians, none apparently eighteen, on poor horses; one waves an old pistol.
Call looks aged: little flesh on his face, beard and mustache flecked with gray.
Clara's note is stained at one corner with dried blood.
Betsey and Sally on the back porch with a toddling Martin between them.
Lorena, blonde, stands by the buggy clutching the letter with her name on it.

Colorado: Denver (telegraph office)
Purgatoire River (the Picketwire), Colorado: night camp where Goodnight appears
Raton Pass, then the New Mexico plain with snow on the Sangre de Cristo peaks to the north

Down the Pecos through the Bosque Redondo, New Mexico

Dry country toward the Colorado (and San Saba) rivers of Texas

Around San Antonio (skirted); across the Nueces

characters: hangman and crowd at Santa Rosa
events: Stung by Clara's words, Call drives south through Kansas in full summer, then veers into Colorado to avoid questions, sending Wilbarger's brother a telegram in Denver.
On the Purgatoire, Charles Goodnight tells him Blue Duck is caught and will hang at Santa Rosa; Call crosses Raton Pass and waits there while the buggy is rebuilt.
Blue Duck taunts Call from his chains, then on hanging day dives through a third-floor courthouse window dragging Deputy Decker to his death; the sheriff hangs the corpse anyway.

Going down the Pecos in drought, Call is shot in the side a day above Horsehead Crossing; the buggy wrecks, he rewraps Gus in a tarp on a travois made of the sign, and Greasy dies before the Colorado.

Call buries Gus under the live oaks above the Guadalupe with the surviving sign plank as marker, scratches A.M. on its back, then rides to Lonesome Dove in August, finding Bolivar ringing the bell and the Dry Bean burned by Wanz.
season: Full summer in Kansas; a dry year on the llano; Call reaches Lonesome Dove late on a day in August, roughly a year after the drive left.
herdPosition: n/a - Call alone with the body; herd remains at the Milk River ranch in Montana.
notes: WHERE CALL IS SHOT: the text says his route ran down the Pecos past Bosque Redondo and on south through New Mexico, then was shot a day above Horsehead Crossing (Horsehead Crossing is in Texas), so the ambush is on the Pecos just north of Horsehead Crossing, likely in Texas; GradeSaver's 'while traveling through New Mexico' is imprecise. The attackers are four unnamed Indians; Call kills one. DENVER: GradeSaver says he rode through Denver to avoid crowds; in the text he turned west into Colorado to avoid the cattle trails, and Denver itself drew a crowd he regretted. GradeSaver/Shmoop say he carried Gus on the mule; the text has a travois made from the sign on the buggy wheels, pulled by Greasy and then by Jerry after Greasy dies. Shmoop says Lonesome Dove is 'nearby' the grave; in fact Call rides south past San Antonio and across the Nueces. Shmoop calls Dillard Brawley 'a cowboy'. Call expected a doctor in Austin but actually skirts San Antonio. The orchard is described only as a hill with live oaks above the Guadalupe (ch96 said the south Guadalupe); the settlers head down the ridge toward San Antonio, which supports placing it in the hill country north of San Antonio. Call says it is five hundred miles from the wreck to the south Guadalupe. Blue Duck's death is here (Santa Rosa, New Mexico). FINAL APPEARANCE: the dinner bell and broken crowbar; the Hat Creek sign (only the company-name line remains; Latin motto lost). Wanz burned the Dry Bean, dying in Lorena's old room with the piano. Ignore trailing table-of-contents junk.

scenes.where: Denver street outside the telegraph office
scenes.action: A crowd fingers the coffin while a shiny undertaker with waxed mustache and blue bow tie offers a ten-dollar funeral.
A big man on a red mule rides up to the fire, declines to dismount, and delivers news of Blue Duck in a few curt lines.
Glass shatters as the chained Blue Duck flies from a third-floor window with Decker, smiling at Call as he falls to the stony ground.

scenes.where: Pecos River bank a day above Horsehead Crossing
scenes.action: A short brown man rises from behind a yucca; Call, bleeding at the side, careens down the bank and the buggy smashes on a rock, coffin underwater.

scenes.where: Hill with live oaks above the Guadalupe; then Lonesome Dove at sunset/dusk
scenes.action: Call rests in the half-dug grave, then plants the splintered sign; weeks later he rides into Lonesome Dove to the clang of the dinner bell beaten by a white-haired Bolivar.

mentionedCharacters: Newt and the boys on the Milk
Xavier Wanz (died burning the Dry Bean)
visualDetails: The Miles City buggy ends up patched so often with wire from trail bosses that it is mostly wire.
Indians along the way include Pawnee, Arapahoe and Ogallala Sioux on horses fat with spring grass.
Goodnight rides a red mule; he has interests in Pueblo.
Santa Rosa courthouse: three stories, gallows at the top, fine glass windows, polished floors; town crowded with cowhands and families sleeping in wagons.
Blue Duck: huge head, snake-cold eyes, larger than Call expected, greasy rag bound round a head wound, shot in shoulder and leg, handcuffed and wrapped in chains bolted to the wall.
Deputy Decker is fat and drunk; Sheriff Owensby is balding and too nervous to eat.
Newspaper boy: red-headed, scarcely twenty, scribbling on a pad.
Llano brown with drought, mirages shimmering, dry lightning at night; the leaking coffin trails fine salt.
Travois: the sign lashed with rope between the two buggy wheels on a salt-cedar axle, Gus wrapped in Call's tarp.

The sign: Latin motto at the bottom broken off, pig and rental lines, Deets's, Pea's and Call's names gone; only the top line naming the Hat Creek Cattle Company and Livery Emporium survives, tied as a crossbar to a mesquite stick; Call scratches A.M. on the back.
Settlers: sunburned beet-red fair young man, wife in a close bonnet, two or three narrow-faced children.
Bolivar: white hair, filthier serape, beating the bell with the broken crowbar; the house is full of cobwebs and rat droppings; the barn is roofless; the stone trough holds clear water.
Dillard Brawley: one-legged barber with a ruined whisper of a voice, carrying a few perch.
